title_en: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
title_fa: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
excerpt_en: Even Healthcare reaches a $300 million valuation in a Khosla Ventures-led round as it plans to expand its hospital network in India.
excerpt_fa: Even Healthcare reaches a $300 million valuation in a Khosla Ventures-led round as it plans to expand its hospital network in India.
content_en:
Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded.
The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million.
Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills.
That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs.
Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services.
“The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said.
Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but co-founder Mayank Banerjee said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary.
“We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch.
Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round.
Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment.
Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes.
The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills.
Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment.
Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. The startup publishes results on its website, alongside figures from other healthcare systems for comparison.
Even says its hospitals have an unplanned readmission rate of less than 1%, compared with an industry benchmark of 8% to 15%. Furthermore, it claims patients spend 40% less time in the hospital and that its approach has saved insurers more than ₹500 million (about $5.27 million).
Jai Sajnani, a partner at Khosla Ventures, told TechCrunch that the early performance of Even’s hospitals was a key reason the firm led the round. “We look forward to helping the Even team put quality care within reach of every family in Bengaluru and across India,” he said.
Even is still losing money, though. The startup posted a net loss of ₹902 million (about $9.50 million) in fiscal 2025, nearly 25% more than the previous year, on revenue of ₹272 million (about $2.86 million), regulatory filings show.
In August, Even also laid off about 350 employees, according to Indian startup-news website Entrackr. Banerjee acknowledged the restructuring and called it a difficult decision. He said the affected employees received severance, extended health insurance, and accelerated equity vesting.
Even currently employs about 650 people, including around 300 doctors full-time. The startup has about 250,000 members and has recorded more than 750,000 patient interactions since its launch in 2021, including consultations, diagnostic tests, and surgeries, Banerjee said.
Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even could turn profitable within months if it stopped spending on expansion, but the startup is choosing to grow instead. He declined to say when the startup expects to become profitable.
“Right now, we’re investing in growth and serving more patients,” Banerjee said.

title_en: What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter?
title_fa: What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter?
excerpt_en: Some router symbols are obvious, while others take a bit of work to decipher. Their lights can vary, too.
excerpt_fa: Some router symbols are obvious, while others take a bit of work to decipher. Their lights can vary, too.
content_en:
What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter?
Depending on their colors, most of those flashing lights are a good sign.
The front of a Netgear router, like many routers, is dotted with a wide array of lights and symbols. Though some of the symbols like the power indicator are straightforward, the lights themselves can be much less clear. They often vary in color; sometimes they're blinking and other times they're solid. If you've never picked up the manual, deciphering what each of the many lights means doesn't come naturally.
Understanding what each of the indicators on your Netgear router signify is important for troubleshooting, as well as making sure everything is running as it should. Although some lights are usually more important than others, they all serve a purpose. Whether you have a standard router or one of the company's mesh Wi-Fi systems, this is how to better understand what your Netgear device is telling you.
The most important lights on your Netgear router
These are the lights on a router that are generally the most important to pay attention to, as they're indicators of the most impactful stats like power and overall internet connection status.
The power LED
Represented by the typical power symbol, this indicates information about your device's firmware, as well as its power status. Unsurprisingly, this will be off if your router has no power.
- Solid green or white: The router is on and ready.
- Solid amber: The router is turning on.
- Blinking amber: The router's firmware is upgrading, or you pressed the reset button.
- Blinking white: The router's firmware is corrupted.
- Blinking white and amber: The router is in access point mode, which means it's acting as a connection point for other devices instead of handling its normal router functions. Some features like VPN and remote management will be unavailable.
If your router isn't working properly, restart it first. In case it's fully unresponsive, you may need to do a factory reset.
Internet LED
The icon and light with a small circle orbiting a larger one shows your general connection status:
- Off: The router is not connected to a modem; check the Ethernet cable to make sure it's fully inserted and not damaged.
- Solid green or white: The internet connection is ready.
- Solid amber: An Ethernet cable connection to the modem has been detected.
- Blinking white: The port is sending and/or receiving traffic.
Wi-Fi LED
Represented by a small dot with two curves on each side, this light shows general Wi-Fi traffic.
- Off: The router's Wi-Fi radios are off.
- Solid white: The router's Wi-Fi radios are operating.
- Blinking white: The router is sending and/or receiving Wi-Fi traffic.
Other lights on your Netgear router
Further lights on your Netgear router are more useful for specific troubleshooting, or if you're plugging additional devices into the router.
Wi-Fi band LEDS
Every modern router should have lights for the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands, as these have long been the standard. For a Wi-Fi 6E model or newer, you'll also see a 6GHz light for that modern band. The lights will differ depending on the bands currently in use, but the lights have the same meanings for each band.
- Off: This particular Wi-Fi radio is off.
- Solid white: The Wi-Fi radio in question is operating.
- Blinking white: The router is sending and/or receiving traffic over the corresponding Wi-Fi radio.
USB LEDs
Your router will have one of these lights for each USB port it includes, represented by the trident USB symbol or the text "USB 3.0."
- Off: No USB device is connected to the port, or the Safely Remove Hardware button was pressed and you're clear to remove the attached device.
- Blinking: A USB device is trying to connect.
- Solid green or white: A USB device is connected and ready to use.
Ethernet LEDs
These are labeled by numbers, with each representing an Ethernet port on the router. The color represents the speed of the connection: white or green for 1 Gbps connections, and amber for slower 100 Mbps or 10 Mbps Ethernet.
- Off: Nothing is connected to the port.
- Solid: A powered-on device is connected to the port.
- Blinking: The port is sending and/or receiving traffic.
WPS LED
Represented by what looks like a router with signals coming out of it, this light indicates the success of a WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) connection, which allows you to add devices to your network without entering the network name and password. For the best router security, you should disable this.
- Off: No WPS connection.
- Blinking: A WPS connection is in progress.
- Solid: The WPS connection was successful.
Reading the lights on a Netgear Orbi mesh system
The lights on Netgear's Orbi Wi-Fi mesh system are minimalist compared to a typical router's, and represent key statuses slightly differently. There's a light in the bottom-front of the device, plus one at the back. The light in the front represents the connection status, while the one at the back is tied to the device's power and firmware.
The front LED lights
- Solid blue light: The connection between the router and satellite is strong.
- Solid amber light: The connection between the router and satellite is OK, but not great.
- Solid magenta light: There's no backhaul connection or no internet connection.
- No light: The Orbi is not receiving power.
The back LED light
- Solid green light: The router and satellite are powered on.
- Solid amber light: The device is rebooting.
- Pulsing amber light: The device is updating its firmware or resetting to factory settings.
- Pulsing red light: Possible hardware issues or connectivity failure.
- No light: The Orbi is not receiving power.

title_en: What does the orange dot on your Samsung Galaxy Watch mean?
title_fa: What does the orange dot on your Samsung Galaxy Watch mean?
excerpt_en: You might sometimes see an orange dot on the left side of your Galaxy Watch's screen. Here's what is tells you.
excerpt_fa: You might sometimes see an orange dot on the left side of your Galaxy Watch's screen. Here's what is tells you.
content_en:
What does the orange dot on your Samsung Galaxy Watch mean?
We have the answer.
Whether you're getting into digital watches for the first time, or transitioning to Galaxy watches from another brand (such as from the Apple Watch Ultra 4 to the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2), Samsung's wrist-worn tech has its fair share of unique attributes. One such feature is the little orange dot that appears to the far left of your watch screen. While it might be a strange quirk if you're not used to it, it's pretty simple to explain.
Throughout the history of the Galaxy Watch, one little orange dot has been a constant. In fact, the dot is present on the latest watch models (including both the Galaxy Watch 8 and the Galaxy Watch 9, as well as the Ultra 2). This little dot is a minimalist way for the Galaxy Watch to display some important information.
The meaning of the Samsung Galaxy Watch's orange dot
The orange dot on Galaxy Watches is a notification indicator — specifically for unread notifications. This dot will remain on your watch's face until you've read all of those outstanding notifications, at which point it will then scurry off. If the dot on your screen is red instead of orange, that means you have an urgent message that you ought to check as soon as possible.
An orange dot is nonetheless common and harmless, but it can be toggled off if it doesn't suit your fancy. Simply head to Settings > Notifications > Advanced Settings and toggle off New notification indicator on watch face. You can also turn the indicator off via a Samsung phone linked to your watch, where you'll simply need to go to the Wearable app and head Watch Settings > Notifications > Advanced notification settings and toggle off New notification indicator on watch face.
Other symbols on the Galaxy Watch
This dot isn't the only symbol of its kind on Galaxy Watches; like with all the best smartwatches, saving space on such a small screen is key to making a solid wearable. While an orange or red dot can be found on the far left of your watch face, other symbols can appear at the top and bottom of the watch. At the top, you might see a phone icon with a slash through it (meaning your watch has lost its Bluetooth connection with your phone), a rectangle with a cloud in the middle (indicating that your watch is connected to your phone with mobile data or Wi-Fi instead of Bluetooth), or a padlock (which means the watch is locked and you'll need your password or PIN to open it).
At the bottom, a blue music note may appear, which tells you whether any app is playing music, as well as if that music is paused — and you can tap the icon to control that audio. Alternatively, a green phone icon could show up in that same spot. This appears when the watch or a connected phone is being used for a call.

title_en: Why you should never point a laser pointer at a security camera
title_fa: Why you should never point a laser pointer at a security camera
excerpt_en: Laser pointers are known to damage security cameras, but do they really? Here's what damage can actually be done.
excerpt_fa: Laser pointers are known to damage security cameras, but do they really? Here's what damage can actually be done.
content_en:
Why you should never point a laser pointer at a security camera
The amount of damage it could do depends on your laser. And your camera.
Opening a door with a hairpin is a common cliché in books, movies and video games. If you are a fan of Better Call Saul, you might have seen a different way of escaping a more technologically advanced capture. In the episode called "Wiedersehen" (Season Four Episode Nine), Werner Ziegler uses a laser pointer to blind a security camera. His escape is only discovered when Mike Ehrmantraut notices some dead pixels on the monitor feeds and finds the pointer. Only it was too late, and Ziegler had already escaped. The trick is clever — but does this work in real life? Well, kind of.
Laser pointers can blind security cameras. In some cases, they can even damage them permanently. However, this would require a combination of three things: a very powerful laser, an older camera and an extremely steady pulse. Possible, but difficult. In most places, it is also illegal. In 2021, a Clearwater man got arrested for pointing a laser at several surveillance cameras owned by the Church of Scientology. The laser did not destroy the cameras, but it did leave dead spots on their lenses, resulting in over $2,000 in damages. Still, the cameras were able to catch him red-handed.
What effect does a laser have on a security camera?
Lasers emit concentrated beams of light at a high intensity. Cameras, meanwhile, are built to convert light into electrical charges, which are then processed and turned into digital video frames. For this reason, security cameras are more susceptible to strong lights than the human eye. Often, exposure to intense light sources such as bright headlights or sunlight reflections can cause the lens to be overwhelmed with light, leading to glare or temporary whiteout effects in footage. Laser pointers can create a similar effect, but stronger.
Most CCTV cameras use either complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) or charge-coupled device (CCD) sensors, which can be targeted directly by laser pointers for a sustained period of time. The laser would overwhelm the camera sensor, temporarily blinding it. Moreover, high-intensity lasers also produce heat. Prolonged exposure to this would result in dead pixels and dark spots in the resulting image. In the worst cases, larger "dead areas" would leave the camera unusable.
Modern cameras are more laser-resistant
Not all lasers can actually damage a camera. It would only be possible with a high-powered laser held still for about 10 seconds. If a laser has an output power under 5mW, it is unlikely to cause anything more than a temporary glare on the camera. The problem? Under US Food and Drug Administration regulations, handheld laser pointers that exceed 5mW of output power are illegal to market, sell or promote. For this reason, anyone with a laser that could actually damage a camera is likely to face larger problems than the damage done to the lens.
Let's say that someone had access to a high-powered laser and pointed it directly at a security camera. Even then, it would be difficult for them to cause real long-term damage. As it turns out, it is not easy to hold one's hand steady and aim straight at a camera lens from a distance for a long time. When researchers at IPVM tried using a laser to blind a security camera, they found it "very difficult" to keep the laser focused on an object from roughly 5 feet away "without their hands shaking off target." At this distance, the team could not cause any permanent damage to the security cameras, regardless of the strength of the laser used.
Even with a high-powered laser and good aim, damaging a modern camera would still be difficult, due to newer technology and sensor protections. Vince Gilligan, co-creator of Better Call Saul, even admitted on a podcast that Ziegler's trick would only work on a camera model from the 1960s.
How to prevent (and address) laser damage in your camera
It is impossible to make a standard home security camera completely laser-proof. However, there are preventative measures that can be taken to protect security cameras and make damaging them more difficult. The key is access.
To laser-proof a camera, the simplest solution is to keep it somewhere high or at an angle. This would make it difficult for anyone to aim at it for a prolonged period, as the IPVM team found. Moving security cameras are also harder to aim at. Additionally, using several cameras to cover the same area increases protection. Overlapping coverage would ensure that there are no blind spots, even if one of the cameras is damaged. Finally, many modern cameras allow the installation of security systems that can detect sudden changes in light or unusual activity. This way, if a camera view is blocked or hit with a bright beam, the system can send an instant phone alert.

In 2021, a Clearwater man got arrested for pointing a laser at several surveillance cameras owned by the Church of Scientology. The laser did not destroy the cameras, but it did leave dead spots on their lenses, resulting in over $2,000 in damages. Still, the cameras were able to catch him red-handed.
What effect does a laser have on a security camera?
Lasers emit concentrated beams of light at a high intensity. Cameras, meanwhile, are built to convert light into electrical charges, which are then processed and turned into digital video frames. For this reason, security cameras are more susceptible to strong lights than the human eye. Often, exposure to intense light sources such as bright headlights or sunlight reflections can cause the lens to be overwhelmed with light, leading to glare or temporary whiteout effects in footage. Laser pointers can create a similar effect, but stronger.
Most CCTV cameras use either complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) or charge-coupled device (CCD) sensors, which can be targeted directly by laser pointers for a sustained period of time. The laser would overwhelm the camera sensor, temporarily blinding it. Moreover, high-intensity lasers also produce heat. Prolonged exposure to this would result in dead pixels and dark spots in the resulting image. In the worst cases, larger "dead areas" would leave the camera unusable.
Modern cameras are more laser-resistant
Not all lasers can actually damage a camera. It would only be possible with a high-powered laser held still for about 10 seconds. If a laser has an output power under 5mW, it is unlikely to cause anything more than a temporary glare on the camera. The problem? Under US Food and Drug Administration regulations, handheld laser pointers that exceed 5mW of output power are illegal to market, sell or promote. For this reason, anyone with a laser that could actually damage a camera is likely to face larger problems than the damage done to the lens.
Let's say that someone had access to a high-powered laser and pointed it directly at a security camera. Even then, it would be difficult for them to cause real long-term damage. As it turns out, it is not easy to hold one's hand steady and aim straight at a camera lens from a distance for a long time. When researchers at IPVM tried using a laser to blind a security camera, they found it "very difficult" to keep the laser focused on an object from roughly 5 feet away "without their hands shaking off target." At this distance, the team could not cause any permanent damage to the security cameras, regardless of the strength of the laser used.
Even with a high-powered laser and good aim, damaging a modern camera would still be difficult, due to newer technology and sensor protections. Vince Gilligan, co-creator of Better Call Saul, even admitted on a podcast that Ziegler's trick would only work on a camera model from the 1960s.
How to prevent (and address) laser damage in your camera
It is impossible to make a standard home security camera completely laser-proof. However, there are preventative measures that can be taken to protect security cameras and make damaging them more difficult. The key is access.
To laser-proof a camera, the simplest solution is to keep it somewhere high or at an angle. This would make it difficult for anyone to aim at it for a prolonged period, as the IPVM team found. Moving security cameras are also harder to aim at. Additionally, using several cameras to cover the same area increases protection. Overlapping coverage would ensure that there are no blind spots, even if one of the cameras is damaged. Finally, many modern cameras allow the installation of security systems that can detect sudden changes in light or unusual activity. This way, if a camera view is blocked or hit with a bright beam, the system can send an instant phone alert.

title_en: How to use Google's SynthID AI detection website
title_fa: How to use Google's SynthID AI detection website
excerpt_en: It's a simple way to check whether an image has been created or manipulated, with a few caveats.
excerpt_fa: It's a simple way to check whether an image has been created or manipulated, with a few caveats.
content_en:
How to use Google's SynthID AI detection website
It's a simple way to check whether an image has been created or manipulated, with a few caveats.
With the proliferation of generative AI tools pumping out images, videos and even songs in recent years, it's hard to spend time on the internet without wondering whether what you're seeing or hearing is real. Google, itself one of the largest purveyors of generative AI, is now making it easier to spot its output. With the new SynthID Detector, anyone can check an image, video, or audio file to see if it's been AI generated, with some major caveats.
Google introduced SynthID in 2023, which adds an imperceptible label to AI-generated content, but there was no way for regular users to actually check for one until now. In 2025, it launched a limited version of SynthID Detector for certain researchers and journalists, and now it's available for everyone. While that may be good news for anyone looking for a way to verify whether a piece of content was generated with AI, it's far from foolproof.
How SynthID Detector works
Since the launch of SynthID, Google's Gemini AI model has embedded a watermark in everything it creates. SynthID Detector works by scanning for that watermark and giving users a simple yes or no answer as to whether one was found. To use the newly available tool, you just need to go to SynthID.com, upload an image, video or audio file, and wait a few seconds for Google to return a result.
That's a big improvement over Google's previous process. Before now, users could ask Gemini itself if a piece of content was AI generated. But for anyone who doesn't trust generative AI, it's hard to take Gemini at its word, and it's an immediate no-go for people who are trying to avoid the technology altogether. SynthID Detector also allows users to scan for watermarks embedded in content created by Google's SynthID partners, which wasn't possible before. That means the new tool can tell whether media was made with AI models from OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao, in addition to Gemini. Apple also participates in SynthID, but support for the detector to identify its creations is still in the works.
How reliable is SynthID Detector?
Since SynthID Detector is simply checking for a watermark rather than analyzing media for patterns that indicate AI use, it should eliminate the chance of false positives. That simplicity introduces its own limitations, though. The most obvious one is that it can't detect media made with AI models that don't use SynthID, such as Meta's tools. SynthID Detector is also limited to telling users whether it finds a label in an uploaded file, without providing any information on what parts of it were AI-generated.
Google says its SynthID signatures persist even if AI generations are edited after being created. While there's no guarantee that an enterprising faker won't find a way around that eventually, the company does seem to be taking steps to avoid that. A Google spokesperson reportedly told Ars Technica that users are limited to around 10 checks per day in order to prevent them from using the detector's output to find a way to remove SynthID. Users also have to be logged in to either a Google, OpenAI, or Apple account to use SynthID Detector.
How does SynthID Detector compare to other AI detectors?
SynthID Detector isn't the only generative AI detector available, but despite its limitations, it's likely one of the most reliable. SynthID partner OpenAI runs its own detector tool, which can pick out AI-confirming metadata as well as SynthID watermarks. Meta embeds its own watermark, called Content Seal, into its AI creations and offers a web-based detector tool, though a 2026 report from Reuters found that it sometimes failed to accurately spot them. Companies like Anthropic and Microsoft have also begun watermarking AI media, but don't currently offer consumer tools to detect them.
The downside of all of these tools is that they're designed to detect a specific AI marker, and no reliable detector exists that can spot generative AI across the board. Many researchers have developed their own AI-spotting tools, but they're not available to the public. And when it comes to the general purpose AI detectors that are openly available, their results are unreliable and prone to flag human-created work as AI content.

title_en: An Xbox Series X can now run PlayStation 5 games, but there's a catch
title_fa: An Xbox Series X can now run PlayStation 5 games, but there's a catch
excerpt_en: The idea of PS5 games running on an Xbox Series X -- made possible by how both consoles were built around closely matched hardware -- is certainly exciting.
excerpt_fa: The idea of PS5 games running on an Xbox Series X -- made possible by how both consoles were built around closely matched hardware -- is certainly exciting.
content_en:
An Xbox Series X can now run PlayStation 5 games, but there’s a catch
What is the PS5X Emulator for Xbox Series X and how does it work?
In a YouTube video that went live on September 8, developer Devran Cosmo Uenal booted the PlayStation 5 version of Quake II on an Xbox Series X and played it with an Xbox controller. But the game was running through PS5X, Uenal's Xbox port of the open-source PS5 emulator KytyPS5, and he has gotten three more PS5 games working alongside it.
The fact that he's managed to get PS5 games running on an Xbox at all is super cool, but there's a catch: PS5X only works in the console's official Developer Mode, where Microsoft's documentation caps games at 5GB of memory. That unfortunately rules out the majority of current-gen games, and there's no public download for anyone else to try yet.
How PS5X works
Sony and Microsoft built their current consoles around closely matched AMD hardware. Both of them have eight Zen 2 CPU cores, RDNA 2 graphics and 16GB of GDDR6 memory, and PS5 games are compiled for the same x86-64 processor architecture that PCs use. That means the KytyPS5 emulator can run their code on the host CPU instead of recreating the PS5's hardware in software. Its developer calls it a compatibility layer and, practically, it behaves more like a translator, converting what a PS5 game asks for into something a PC can understand.
KytyPS5 translates the PS5's graphics commands and recompiles its shaders for Vulkan. As a result, it needs a Vulkan 1.3 graphics card on PC, but Xbox Developer Mode only supports DirectX 11 and DirectX 12. "Since Vulkan isn't supported, everything needs to be translated to DirectX," Uenal wrote in the YouTube video's description, where he also admitted that AI was involved in the work. As VideoCardz pointed out, that means fixes the KytyPS5 team makes to its PC renderer have to be adapted before PS5X can use them.
Uenal's video also describes PS5X as a "research project" for "running PS5 homebrew and game backups" on a Series X in Developer Mode. He claims that it doesn't include any PS5 firmware or decryption keys, and KytyPS5's documentation tells users to stick to game files they've obtained legally. Dodging copy protection is ultimately what killed the Switch emulator Yuzu, whose makers settled a Nintendo lawsuit back in 2024 by paying $2.4 million and shutting the project down. The team behind the PS3 emulator RPCS3 lists KytyPS5 and SharpEmu as the two active open-source PS5 emulators that can boot games, and warns players about scam sites posing as real ones.
What PS5X can run
At the time of writing, PS5X runs the PS5 versions of GEX Trilogy, Hellboy: Web of Wyrd, Marvel Cosmic Invasion and Quake II, and all four are compatible with Xbox controller inputs. Some of them have working sound, and TweakTown reckons that Quake II runs at roughly 25 to 45 frames per second in Uenal's footage. It's worth noting that these four games are also sold on other platforms, so there's no sign yet of PS5X running a PS5 exclusive, and Uenal admits that it's early days and that compatibility is limited.
Android Authority reported on September 28 that KytyPS5 now goes in-game in a variety of PS5 titles on PC, and that one user had shown Marvel's Wolverine reaching its main menu, in slow motion, on a machine with an NVIDIA RTX 5090. That clip didn't show any gameplay, however, and it's not clear whether it used the standard emulator build. PS5 emulation on PC is becoming more viable by the week, but it's still an extremely nascent field, and PS5X only inherits any progress once each fix has been rebuilt for DirectX and squeezed into a far smaller memory budget.
Developer Mode's memory limit
Microsoft limits games in Developer Mode to a relatively small 5GB of memory, and apps to 1GB. Requests for more memory than that allocation fail. In contrast, a retail Series X game gets 13.5GB of the console's 16GB, while the remainder is reserved for the console's OS. That leaves PS5X to work with about 37 percent of the memory a normal Xbox game can use, making it an obvious no-go for big current-gen releases. Microsoft only lifts this cap when software runs via the Visual Studio debugger, which is a setup designed for devs testing their code.
Microsoft blocked emulators entirely in Xbox's normal retail mode back in 2023, its rationale for doing so being a store policy that bans products that emulate a game system. It then started bringing down the ban hammer and reportedly handed out 15-day suspensions to players who found a workaround. Since then, players who want to play PS2 or GameCube games through, say, Dolphin, the most popular GameCube emulator, have had to rely on Developer Mode instead. But a console in that mode can't load retail games until it's switched back.
Xbox Series X comes with the same Zen 2 architecture and RDNA 2 graphics as a PS5. It's also got the same amount of memory, and PS5X can use less than a third of that. But none of this really matters because of the memory cap. There's no real workaround to this without a jailbreak, meaning Xbox players won't benefit from the progress being made on the PC. Sure, PS5X is interesting, but it'll remain a cool little curio rather than anything substantive players can use.
If you're interested in checking out PS5X and similar emulation projects, you should exercise caution. Scammers are capitalizing on the interest these projects receive, such as releasing malware under similar names like PCS5X to try and trick players into downloading it.

title_en: Starlink has two $55 plans that are wildly different — here's how
title_fa: Starlink has two $55 plans that are wildly different — here's how
excerpt_en: It's a trade-off between download speeds and data caps.
excerpt_fa: It's a trade-off between download speeds and data caps.
content_en:
Starlink has two $55 plans that are wildly different — here's how
It's a trade-off between download speeds and data caps.
SpaceX's Starlink has gone through a number of changes over the years when it comes to the different types of satellite-powered internet plans you can subscribe to. But nowadays, the company has settled on a more streamlined offering with its Residential and Roam plans, both of which start at $55 per month.
If you already own a Starlink dish or are willing to rent one through the company itself, you may be wondering which plan you should go with. Despite costing the same amount, the entry-level Residential and Roam tiers aren't interchangeable and choosing one or the other heavily depends on your living situation and what you need the internet for.
We'll breakdown what comes with each tier and the type of people they're best suited for. Note that we're just covering Starlink's Personal plans for individuals and families; the Business plans offer completely different services.
Comparing Residential and Roam
As the name implies, the Residential plan is for those who could use the service in their homes, or at least a fixed location where they're living long-term. All the Residential tiers come with unlimited data, and the big difference between them is how fast your internet speed is.
The basic $55 tier gives you 100 Mbps, which roughly translates to 12.5 megabytes per second for downloading (you can divide your internet speed by eight to get an idea of download times). That's good enough for a small household to browse, stream movies and play games online.
The other two tiers in Residential increase your speed — 200 Mbps for $85 a month, or up to 400 Mbps in Max for $130 — and both get you free professional home installation as well.
Starlink describes the Roam plan as "best for RVs, nomads, and campers, and working on the go," including international travelers. This is the one to choose if you have or plan to own a Starlink Mini dish that you can easily pack in a bag. Unlike the speed-based model in the Residential plans, the basic tiers in Roam give you hard data caps with high-speed internet.
For the $55 tier, you get 100GB per month with speeds of up to 300 Mbps. Once you hit that cap, your connection significantly slows down — just enough for some basic browsing and emailing until your plan renews again. The remaining tiers offer a higher data cap (300GB for $80 a month) and the Unlimited option that removes the cap altogether for $175 a month.
One thing to keep in mind with both Residential and Roam is that you may not always get the advertised speeds on a consistent basis. Starlink's fair use policy states it may temporarily reduce speeds during times of high congestion or peak usage hours in your area.
Before you choose a plan, you can check Starlink's coverage map to see what type of download speeds are available in your state or country. Both types of plans also come with a 30-day trial that allows you to get a full refund within the first month if you aren't satisfied with the internet service.

title_en: Router and modem or gateway: What's actually in your home network?
title_fa: Router and modem or gateway: What's actually in your home network?
excerpt_en: A gateway pulls double duty, but a modem and router combo can give you a lot more flexibility and power.
excerpt_fa: A gateway pulls double duty, but a modem and router combo can give you a lot more flexibility and power.
content_en:
Router and modem or gateway: What's actually in your home network?
Understand the networking equipment that connects your devices to the internet.
Don't feel bad for being unfamiliar with home networking terms. Many concepts aren't relevant for most people until they need to fix problems with their home network. The goal is for your network to blend seamlessly into the background, just as you don't think much about carburetors or batteries when driving your car.
However, understanding your network is helpful not just for troubleshooting, but also for being aware of what you're paying for and deciding what you actually need. It's long been common for internet service providers (ISPs) to charge rental fees for equipment, though this has thankfully been fading in recent years. If your ISP still charges a fee, you can potentially save money by buying your own. Even if a unit is included in your plan, bringing your own can unlock more flexibility and options.
Let's walk through the basic differences between a router, modem and gateway. They're not hard to understand, even though some companies seem to intentionally blur the lines.
Routers and modems and gateways, oh my!
The vast majority of internet connections are dependent on a modem (short for modulator-demodulator). That hardware translates the signals from a cable or phone line into a digital form your devices can understand, as well as vice-versa. For an even simpler definition, a modem is the device that talks to the internet. The only way you can potentially skip having some sort of modem is if you have a pure fiber connection. Those replace the modem with an optical network terminal (ONT), which is functionally the same type of device from a practical standpoint.
Routers have multiple responsibilities. Primarily, they steer modem data to (and from) individual devices, whether that's over Wi-Fi or Ethernet cables. But they can also direct entirely local data on your home network, like if you're streaming movies from a Plex server to your TV. Some routers additionally serve as smart home hubs by acting as Matter controllers or bridging Thread-based accessories with your local network and the internet. All the while, they defend your network against intrusion and malware through measures like firewalls. You can also manually manage traffic using tools like user profiles and guest networks.
Within a home networking context, a gateway usually merges a modem and router into a single device. The obvious advantage of this is simplicity, with ISPs frequently including a gateway (increasingly at no additional charge) in your monthly plan. You won't see as many of these at normal retailers, incidentally. Gateways available from stores are often aimed at businesses and other organizations looking for advanced control over incoming and outgoing data. You might come across combo gateways, but it's usually more advantageous to go with separate units for each.
Why you should almost always buy your own router
Whether your ISP provides you with a gateway or a separate modem and router, you're likely getting a cheap, lowest-common-denominator networking setup for a modern home. That could mean Wi-Fi 6, and it almost certainly means a non-mesh configuration. The vast majority of internet connections are dependent on a modem (short for modulator-demodulator). The obvious advantage of this is simplicity, with ISPs frequently including a gateway (increasingly at no additional charge) in your monthly plan. You won't see as many of these at normal retailers, incidentally. content_en:
Now, former Savannah police officer Amber Harpe was fired in August following a department investigation that found she had shared her Flock login information with her husband, Tyler Harpe, an ICE agent. SPD does not share its Flock data with ICE and said sharing access to the system violated the department’s security protocols.
A Savannah police officer gave her Flock login to her ICE agent husband
SPD officer Amber Harpe was fired for sharing her Flock access with her ICE agent husband.
SPD officer Amber Harpe was fired for sharing her Flock access with her ICE agent husband.
While he had unauthorized access to the system, Tyler Harpe conducted 983 searches related to 97 license plates, which were overwhelmingly registered to Hispanic drivers, according to Savannah’s local ABC affiliate, WJCL. The Harpes defended their actions, saying they didn’t use access for personal reasons and that the searches were strictly for “law-enforcement purposes.”
Interim Major Max Nowinsky originally recommended a light eight-hour suspension for Harpe. However, Major Michelle Halford and Assistant Police Chief Robert Gavin disagreed, and they removed her from the force. Harpe was fired, along with five other SPD employees, after an internal investigation uncovered Flock misuse. Four of them were later arrested; however, Harpe was not one of them.

title_en: What is Apple's Image Playground app for and how do you use it?
title_fa: What is Apple's Image Playground app for and how do you use it?
excerpt_en: Apple's image generation tool got some noteworthy updates this fall.
excerpt_fa: Apple's image generation tool got some noteworthy updates this fall.
content_en:
What is Apple's Image Playground app for and how do you use it?
Apple's image generation tool got some noteworthy updates this fall.
Sometimes, a text exchange with a friend calls for a super specific image to express a thought. It's the kind of image that you can't find in the legion of emoji on your phone, or hiding in your photo library — an angry avocado, or a picture of you and that friend on the moon when you've never even been out of the city together. The human experience is complex.
In times like these, you might turn to an AI image generator to meet your needs. For those in the Apple ecosystem, one option is firing up the Image Playground app as a quick way of creating an image that can be customized, saved and even used as a Genmoji in the future. (Genmoji are personalized emoji you can make using Apple Intelligence.)
If you haven't used the app, odds are it's already your phone. Here's a rundown of what Apple's Image Playground is and how to use it.
What is Apple's Image Playground?
Apple initially launched Image Playground in December 2024. The app uses Apple Intelligence to generate images on your device that you can save, share or turn into Genmoji. Image Playground is integrated into several Apple apps, like Messages, Keynote and Freeform, so you don't have to stop what you're doing and open another app separately.
To use Image Playground, you'll need an iPhone 15 Pro or Pro Max, or an iPhone 16 or later with Apple Intelligence turned on. You can also use it on iPads with an M1 chip or later, or the iPad Mini (A17 Pro), as well as Macs with at least an M1 chip.
The latest version of Image Playground, available with iOS 27, brings a few updates to the app. Perhaps the most notable is that you can now describe what visual style you're looking for with natural language. Earlier versions of the app let you select a few specific (like illustration), but the new "Any Style" option lets you specify "virtually" any visual approach. Other updates include modifying what you've already created with touch and natural language. So, if you ask for an image of a cabin, you can use your finger to select the door, and prompt Playground to change it to red, or even move the selection around. The update also introduces the ability to make Contact Posters and wallpapers for your Lock Screen.
How do you use it?
When you open the app, there are several ways you can go about creating an image. If you're starting from scratch, you can use the prompt box to describe what you want to make. There's also a menu you can expand featuring styles, like animation and sketch. If you select Genmoji from that list, you'll be able to save your creation along with any other stickers you have, and use it as you would an emoji.
There are other ways to start images, too, beyond entering a natural language prompt. Near the prompt box, you can tap the figure of a person, and select a face from one of your photos. For example, if you pick yourself, you can change which photo you want to use as the reference image, and prompt Playground to maybe show you as an astronaut. Below the image, you can enter additional prompts to make changes or use the touch feature to tweak the image.
Similarly, next to the icon of the person, there's a button that lets you use a photo you've taken as the basis for the image. When you're happy with you hath wrought, you can tap the Share button and unleash it on your friends and loved ones.

title_en: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
title_fa: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
excerpt_en: Benchmark may have grown its funds and swapped out some partners, but onstage the five who are left sounded like friends who just happen to be running one of the Valley’s most storied firms
excerpt_fa: Benchmark may have grown its funds and swapped out some partners, but onstage the five who are left sounded like friends who just happen to be running one of the Valley’s most storied firms
content_en:
The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle.
But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria.
Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article.
Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark?
Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part.
[As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye. A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus.
Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund?
Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight.
Ev, you joined Benchmark late last year. You’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ?
Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes that are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team.
And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other. That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer.
Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark?
Jack Altman: It’s funny. I did the podcast with these guys at the start of this year, and during that podcast, obviously we talked about the commitment to being a small fund, but more than that, what I heard was that they want to be the first people who founders call, they want to be concentrated, and they just care. So much in this industry gets tied up in money and status, and what I felt from the Benchmark team then, and ten times more as I’ve gotten to know them so well, is it’s a group that really cares about founders and helping companies. And I did enjoy being an individual investor. . .but in a market this crazy, I don’t know how I’d feel, figuring it out on my own. Having a group of people who are so smart and focused and driven to learn it with and from has been awesome. There’s no better place to learn.
I’m told you meet on Mondays with no agenda.
Chethan Puttagunta: Jack tried to make an agenda. [Laughs.]
Altman: I’ve got an agenda for next Monday.
Eric Vishria: It’s weirdly arbitrary, honestly. It’s an ongoing conversation. In a time of rapid change, you’re trying to figure out what’s becoming possible that wasn’t possible six months ago, and who’s bending light. We talk about what companies we’re meeting, what piqued our interest and why, what we’re seeing in board meetings. You can try to systematize it, but one of the beauties of five people is you don’t have to. It’s a decades-long conversation that only works if you’re small and actually enjoy spending time together. After this session, we’re having dinner with one of the very few entrepreneurs who has built a multi-hundred-billion-dollar company, someone we’re not invested in, just to stretch our thinking.
Puttagunta: Part of not having an agenda is you need space to be reactive. If a founder needs help landing an executive or a strategic partnership, the five of us can be at their disposal.
You’re an equal partnership. Can one person put the kibosh on a deal?
Puttagunta: Nobody knows. We don’t have rules around it.
Altman: I actually don’t...

title_en: Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’
title_fa: Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’
excerpt_en: Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund.
excerpt_fa: Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund.
content_en:
Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good.
Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.”
There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study. But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”
Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.”
If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months.

title_en: After five years, Inscryption is finally coming to mobile
title_fa: After five years, Inscryption is finally coming to mobile
excerpt_en: The studio celebrated Inscryption's five-year anniversary with a Twitch stream.
excerpt_fa: The studio celebrated Inscryption's five-year anniversary with a Twitch stream.
content_en:
After five years, Inscryption is finally coming to mobile
There's really no escaping now.
The team behind the hit horror card game Inscryption shared some exciting news this weekend in celebration of its fifth anniversary: a mobile version is on the way. The announcement came during an official Twitch stream, which featured an appearance by Inscryption creator Daniel Mullins. It's still going to be a little while until it hits the app stores as the team works to get it right, but you'll soon be able to bring Inscryption and its strange cast of creatures and Scrybes with you everywhere.
If you were hoping to see some new DLC with this announcement, well, sorry. Daniel Mullins Games confirmed that no such content updates are coming as of now. In a post on Reddit, the team explained that "we feel that Inscryption is a complete experience, both narratively and gameplay-wise. We don't want to add content simply for the sake of adding more, or to capitalize on the game's success. Preserving the atmosphere, identity, and experience that made Inscryption special in the first place is incredibly important to us."
We can expect to hear more about Inscryption's mobile release in the coming months. The team is primarily focused right now on getting Pony Island 2 out the door. Daniel Mullins Games recently announced that the highly anticipated followup to 2016's Pony Island will hit Steam on April 27, 2027.

If you were hoping to see some new DLC with this announcement, well, sorry. Daniel Mullins Games confirmed that no such content updates are coming as of now. In a post on Reddit, the team explained that "we feel that Inscryption is a complete experience, both narratively and gameplay-wise. We don't want to add content simply for the sake of adding more, or to capitalize on the game's success. Preserving the atmosphere, identity, and experience that made Inscryption special in the first place is incredibly important to us."
We can expect to hear more about Inscryption's mobile release in the coming months. The team is primarily focused right now on getting Pony Island 2 out the door. Daniel Mullins Games recently announced that the highly anticipated followup to 2016's Pony Island will hit Steam on April 27, 2027.

title_fa: Mister Organ is one of the most unsettling documentaries I’ve ever seen
excerpt_en: Mister Organ doesn't reach the level of societal horror of The Act of Killing or the creepypasta-meets-true-crime gruesomeness of Beware the Slenderman, but there's something deeply unsettling about Michael Organ and his intimate campaign of terror against everyone who enters...
excerpt_fa: Mister Organ doesn't reach the level of societal horror of The Act of Killing or the creepypasta-meets-true-crime gruesomeness of Beware the Slenderman, but there's something deeply unsettling about Michael Organ and his intimate campaign of terror against everyone who enters...
content_en:
Mister Organ doesn’t reach the level of societal horror of The Act of Killing or the creepypasta-meets-true-crime gruesomeness of Beware the Slenderman, but there’s something deeply unsettling about Michael Organ and his intimate campaign of terror against everyone who enters his life.
Mister Organ is one of the most unsettling documentaries I’ve ever seen
The story of Michael Organ is the rare documentary that doubles as a psychological horror film.
The story of Michael Organ is the rare documentary that doubles as a psychological horror film.
Mister Organ is a documentary by David Farrier, an Auckland, New Zealand journalist. The movie starts with Farrier reporting on Bashford Antiques, a shop in Ponsonby that has begun aggressively clamping cars in its lot and demanding exorbitant fees to release them — up to $760. Farrier’s article for The Spinoff eventually led the government to introduce legislation that would outlaw extreme clamping fees.
Under normal circumstances, that would be the end of the story. But at the center of this story is a man named Michael Organ who turns out to be a bizarre, seemingly dangerous conman.
Organ was hired to police Bashford’s lot, and during his investigation, Farrier discovers he’s more than just a parking-lot bully. Years earlier, Organ had been charged with attempting to steal a yacht in an elaborate scheme. What’s more, he claimed to be a prince and a lawyer — he is neither.
As Farrier talks to people who have known Organ and interacts with him directly, what emerges is a portrait of a deeply troubled man who has left a trail of traumatized people in his wake. The movie shifts from a wild portrait of a conman to something more alarming and tense when Organ reveals he’s gotten his hands on a key to Farrier’s home and only warns him to be careful.
From there it spirals even further; eventually, Farrier felt it necessary to leave the country to protect himself from Organ’s campaign of harassment and gaslighting. It’s the rare documentary that doubles as a psychological horror film.

title_en: Everyone’s watching the Elizabeth Holmes documentary ‘You Can See Everything’
title_fa: Everyone’s watching the Elizabeth Holmes documentary ‘You Can See Everything’
excerpt_en: "You Can See Everything" is having the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film.
excerpt_fa: "You Can See Everything" is having the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film.
content_en:
“You Can See Everything” is already a box office sensation, with a $15 million opening weekend (based on Sunday estimates). That’s the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film.
The nearly three-hour movie — first revealed last month at a secretive screening at the Telluride Film Festival — is only playing in 855 theaters this weekend. (In contrast, the weekend’s number one movie, “Street Fighter,” is playing in 3,575.) But it had a reported 2,000 sellout screenings, and the reviews are overwhelmingly positive; “You Can See Everything” currently has a score of 99% on both Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic.
The story of Elizabeth Holmes’ rise and fall — founding blood-testing startup Theranos, attracting support from many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names, then ultimately being sentenced to 11 years in prison for defrauding investors — has already been told in books, podcasts, TV shows, and other documentaries.
But “You Can See Everything”’s filmmakers were given extensive access to Holmes and her family in the month before she went to jail, and the involvement of “The Rehearsal” creator Nathan Fielder — who co-directed the film with Lance Oppenheim — made the whole thing even more intriguing.
While I haven’t seen the movie myself, I can at least attest to the difficulty of finding tickets in Manhattan: I spent a good chunk of yesterday trying to find a screening for tonight, and I found exactly one with seats available that weren’t in the front row. (Yes, of course I’m going.)
TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling already got to see it on Thursday. She wrote that the enigmatic Holmes finally seems to have met her match in Fielder, a deadpan comedian who’s arguably just as strange and mysterious as she is. Fielder’s month with Holmes is apparently just the beginning of what sounds like an increasingly surreal, metatextual odyssey.
The discussion around “You Can See Everything” may be making it harder for other tech-centric films to break through. Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Network” follow-up “The Social Reckoning” opened to a disappointing $5.5 million last weekend, and has already fallen entirely out of the top 10. And Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” — hampered, perhaps, by resistance from social platforms and a four-hour runtime — made only $306,702 this weekend.

title_en: What is the star button for on your Roku remote?
title_fa: What is the star button for on your Roku remote?
excerpt_en: While the Roku remote doesn't have confusing colors or weird symbols, the star button can confuse some folks at first.
excerpt_fa: While the Roku remote doesn't have confusing colors or weird symbols, the star button can confuse some folks at first.
content_en:
What is the star button for on your Roku remote?
Roku's remote is straightforward, except for its multi-purpose star button.
A Roku system's remote control is one of the most straightforward remote designs you'll find. The function behind nearly every button is clear from its icon, except for one: the mysterious star button that lurks above the fast forward button. Whether you're using the physical remote or the remote in the Roku mobile app, you're going to encounter it — but what is it for?
Its purpose isn't as cut and dry as something like the OK or Netflix button, because its usage is contextual depending on when you press it. It's essentially a mix of an "options" button and accessibility shortcut, with some functionality depending on whether you have a Roku TV or one of the company's streaming boxes. Once you know all the scenarios where you can utilize it, you'll be able to improve several facets of your Roku watching experience.
Everything the Roku star button can do
What the star button does is dependent upon where you are on your Roku device. Let's consider the three major ones.
On the home screen
When you're on the Roku home screen, the star button's functionality depends on whether you're in the Quick Access section or the general app selection screen. In Quick Access, hitting star while an app is highlighted will only give you the option to remove it from the section; in the full apps list you'll have more options.
When you have an app highlighted there, pressing the star will show you the app's version and build number, let you move the channel's positioning or remove it, rate the app, give feedback or check for app updates. On a Roku TV, if you highlight an external device like a video game console, you'll be given the option to rename it.
When watching something
If you're actively streaming video on your Roku TV, the star button opens a host of viewing options in a sidebar. Here, you can improve your Roku's image quality, set a sleep timer, turn on closed captioning, change the volume mode and much more. The specific options will vary slightly from app to app based on their capabilities, but in general, this is the place to precisely tailor your viewing experience. On a Roku streaming box, this menu won't hold as many options as a Roku TV does.
As an accessibility shortcut
Some Roku devices support a text-to-speech screen reader (formerly called Audio Guide), an accessibility feature that helps navigation. This feature is currently only available in the United States. Roku devices that support the screen reader include:
- Roku TV
- Roku Streambar and Streambar Pro
- Roku Smart Soundbar
- Roku Express and Express+
- Roku Express 4K and 4K+
- Roku Streaming Stick and Streaming Stick+
- Roku Streaming Stick 4K and 4K+
- Roku Premiere and Premiere+
- Roku Ultra and Ultra LT
Though the screen reader can be activated via the accessibility settings menu, you can also toggle it by quickly pressing the star button four times in a row. To adjust controls like the precise speech rate and volume of the screen reader, you'll need to go to the Accessibility category of the Settings page, but the star button allows you to activate the feature without venturing into menus.

title_en: Here's how the Slate truck gets software updates without built-in infotainment
title_fa: Here's how the Slate truck gets software updates without built-in infotainment
excerpt_en: Basically, it's on you.
excerpt_fa: Basically, it's on you.
content_en:
Here's how the Slate truck gets software updates without built-in infotainment
Using your phone to phone home.
The Slate truck doesn't just lack an infotainment system. The base version of the EV also skips a radio, speakers, power windows and even a paint job (hello, vinyl). But without built-in cellular, the truck can still get over-the-air (OTA) software updates. It does so by piggybacking on your device.
Maximum minimalism
Slate Auto's approach to minimalism isn't just a design choice. It's also the core of the company's business model: it reaches its sub-$25,000 entry price by slashing everything unrelated to driving and safety.
Of course, the company will still be happy to sell you a long list of add-ons to fill those missing pieces. These include speakers, an iPad mount (to turn it into something more like a traditional infotainment system), a kit that transforms it into a five-seat SUV and a telematics module that enables in-app door unlocking. All that can add up, with a fully loaded version of the modular vehicle surpassing $45,000. The upsell temptation could be strong.
The EV has an estimated 205 miles of range, a 1,550-pound maximum payload and a 2,000-pound tow rating. It's designed more for short-run hauling and errands than long road trips, so it isn't an apples-to-apples comparison with other electric trucks. Still, the company is betting that a surprisingly affordable vehicle that cuts corners on luxuries will find its niche.
How updates work
Typically, OTA software updates use cellular or Wi-Fi. But the Slate truck's lack of tech means it needs a workaround.
The process happens through the Slate app on your phone. When an update is available, the app downloads it onto your device. Plug your phone into the truck's USB port on the dash, and wait for the initial file transfer (the part where your phone needs to be connected). That takes about a minute. Then the truck finishes installing on its own, a step that can take around 45 minutes.
The company says the updates will stick to bug fixes and small improvements, so don't expect big, flashy new features to arrive after installation. And the same app you use for updates also helps with other common tasks, like displaying range, helping you find chargers and passing those directions to Google Maps, Apple Maps or Waze.
Privacy
A truck that doesn't phone home could attract buyers tired of the techification of all things. So it probably helps Slate's case that it says it won't sell app data and only collects what it needs for things like diagnostics, service and update status. Those familiar with the recent GM data selling debacle could see the allure here.
Whether enough buyers want an electric pickup that scales back on so much is an open question. But at least the software will still stay up-to-date for those who do.

title_en: A woman was arrested in Philly for blocking a delivery robot
title_fa: A woman was arrested in Philly for blocking a delivery robot
excerpt_en: Carolyn Marvin was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct after blocking the path of an Uber delivery robot and refusing to get out of the way. Marvin told Philadelphia's ABC13 "I know they're taking the jobs of human delivery workers and so, I have been protesting them...
excerpt_fa: Carolyn Marvin was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct after blocking the path of an Uber delivery robot and refusing to get out of the way. Marvin told Philadelphia's ABC13 "I know they're taking the jobs of human delivery workers and so, I have been protesting them...
content_en:
Carolyn Marvin was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct after blocking the path of an Uber delivery robot and refusing to get out of the way. Marvin told Philadelphia’s ABC13 “I know they’re taking the jobs of human delivery workers and so, I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward.”
A woman was arrested in Philly for blocking a delivery robot
Carolyn Marvin was charged with ‘disorderly conduct’ for protesting delivery robots taking jobs.
Carolyn Marvin was charged with ‘disorderly conduct’ for protesting delivery robots taking jobs.
Police responded to the scene and asked Marvin to move out of the robot’s way. When she refused, they placed her in cuffs and arrested her. The incident was captured on video and has now garnered considerable media attention.
The delivery robots have become a common sight on the streets of downtown Philadelphia and have sparked backlash. This is not even Marvin’s first brush with them. And earlier this year, one was kicked over in Center City. Broad concern has grown about how autonomous systems, including robotaxis, delivery robots, and AI agents, are impacting jobs, especially for lower-skill workers.

title_en: From the Royole FlexPai to the iPhone Duo: How the modern foldable phone has evolved
title_fa: From the Royole FlexPai to the iPhone Duo: How the modern foldable phone has evolved
excerpt_en: Apple's iPhone Duo likely forecasts a shift in the market toward foldables becoming more common. But it took a while to get here.
excerpt_fa: Apple's iPhone Duo likely forecasts a shift in the market toward foldables becoming more common. But it took a while to get here.
content_en:
From the Royole FlexPai to the iPhone Duo: How the modern foldable phone has evolved
Are foldables finally ready to go mainstream?
Technological advances often come with growing pains. This is no less true of phones. The 1984 "brick" phone (DynaTAC 8000X) required users to carry over 1.7 pounds of weight for only half an hour of talk time, at a hefty price tag of $3,995. Foldable phones are not so troublesome, but I still struggled to fit the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 4 in my pocket when I first got it. What's more, the size of it kept prompting friends to ask why I was carrying two phones around. I wish I had been, for at least it would mean one would have a decent camera. Still, the moment when the phone unfolded and the screen adjusted to the larger size was as awe-inspiring back then as it is now.
Today, after having gotten my hands on some newer models, I have become very impressed by the lengths foldable technology has reached. Models including the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 have propelled the technology forward. Even Apple has decided to enter the market, with the iPhone Duo launch that has everyone talking. Suddenly, the future uptake of foldable phones is almost a certainty. Apple might well end up having everything to do with this change, but it would not have been possible without the long list of breakthroughs — and failures — that came before it.
The first stumbles: Royole, Samsung and Huawei
Trend pieces declared 2019 the "year of the foldable." It was not, though those 12 months did provide the first meaningful strides in the technology. The first device of this type to make a splash in the headlines was designed by an unknown Chinese display manufacturer: Royole. The company presented the FlexPai at CES 2019, with all the pomp and circumstance that "the world's first commercially available foldable smartphone" required. It was a feat of technology. It captivated the audience, if only momentarily. For all its charms, Engadget's reporters at the time found the Royole FlexPai to be "rough around the edges," strangely sized and, overall, "janky." Regardless, it demonstrated that flexible OLED could ship in a real product.
Later that year came a second attempt. Samsung's first Galaxy Fold was released in February 2019, kick-starting a series of unfortunate events for the phone manufacturer. If you were there, you might remember the influx of terrible reviews that followed. Despite a high price (just under $2,000), many reviewers complained that their phone screens had broken after little use, and it was revealed that most of them had peeled off a layer of plastic that was acting as a screen protector. The phone's fragility forced Samsung to delay the public launch and recall all units sent to reviewers so it could re-engineer the product. The new version was, however, only "somewhat" more sturdy. Overall, those first Samsung phones showed the importance of perfecting the crease, hinge durability and screen resistance as key to the success of foldable phones.
The next step showed the route not taken. Huawei's Mate X, presented at MWC 2019, folded outward instead of inward. It used a single high-resolution display that wrapped around the outside of the phone. The resulting design was extremely elegant. The problem? The screen could easily be scratched and damaged. On top of that, the phone was never sold in the United States due to the sanctions imposed by then-President Donald Trump on Chinese technologies. Still, for as striking as the Mate X was, the company's next foldable, the Mate X2, used the inward fold introduced by Royole and Samsung, showing that different does not necessarily mean better.
The Android maturity years
The years between 2020 and 2025 gave way to an avalanche of foldable phone models, pushed by Android phone makers. Almost every phone released over these years came with a significant advance. It was all this hard work that has made the foldable phone viable. Still, no specific model achieved what the manufacturers truly wanted: to make the foldable phone mainstream.
At first, foldable phone makers were mainly concerned with protecting the screens against pressure, water and dust. In 2020, Samsung's Galaxy Z Flip introduced ultra-thin glass in the inner screen, making it more robust. The Z Fold 3 and Z Flip 3, released in 2021, came with IPX8 water resistance. Dust was harder to protect against than water, but still the Fold 6 came with partial dust protection (IP48). In 2025, Google's Pixel 10 Pro Fold reached full IP68. The other big battle was how to address the crease. It was Oppo, with its 2021 Find N, that achieved a near-invisible crease. After that, Honor's Magic V series kept cutting thickness until Samsung answered with the slim Galaxy Z Fold 7.
The other element that needed to change for the technology to be widespread was pricing. Over this period, clamshell phones like the rebooted Motorola Razr and the $999 Galaxy Z Flip 3 brought prices down to regular flagship levels, making foldable phones better for everyone's physical and figurative pockets.
Apple comes to town
Can Apple make the final push that will take foldable phones into the mainstream? It has done it before and could, no doubt, do it again if the iPhone Duo is everything that has been promised.
During its history, Apple has mastered the ability to wait until the first hiccups of a technology have passed before entering a market and disrupting it. The company did it with touchscreens, and again with foldable phones, waiting until the crease problem that Samsung struggled with had been resolved before putting out its own model. In 2026, the announcement finally arrived in the form of the iPhone Duo. Folded, the phone is passport-sized. It has a 7.6-inch internal display and a 5.4-inch external display, at a starting price of $1,999. Overall, it has all the ingredients to be a huge success, with reviewers deeming the iPhone Duo Apple's "most exciting device...
