title_en: You might be surprised by how much the Slate truck can carry
title_fa: You might be surprised by how much the Slate truck can carry
excerpt_en: Don't underestimate this compact pickup.
excerpt_fa: Don't underestimate this compact pickup.
content_en:
You might be surprised by how much the Slate truck can carry
Don't underestimate this compact pickup.
The perpetual cry of the growing number of EV fans is that most models are too expensive here in North America. A compact like the temporarily revived Chevy Bolt starts at $27,600 before any upgrades, and naturally, a lot of drivers need more passenger or cargo space. An EV like the Rivian R2 might as well be a Ferrari in an economy where house ownership is a major hurdle.
Enter the Slate truck, shipping toward the very end of 2026. It not only starts at $24,950, but it also offers one of the most popular form factors in the US: the pickup truck. You do have to spend more than that if you want basic creature comforts, yet that price tag is actually better than most gas-guzzling alternatives. The cheapest Ford F-150 starts north of $40,000 — so even an upgraded Slate could be a smarter financial decision.
Naturally, a question potential buyers are going to have is how much cargo such a cheap truck can possibly carry. The answer is surprisingly reassuring, even if Slate isn't going to be replacing Ford or Dodge on the most demanding construction sites with the likes of a 2,000-pound towing limit.
The scoop on the Slate's towing and payload specs
Let's cut to the chase. The Slate has a 5-foot-long truck bed, capable of holding 35.1 cubic feet, assuming you don't install any mods to extend usable area. That's shorter than the 5.5-foot bed on the cheapest 2026 F-150, and shallower too, since the F-150 supports up to 52.8 cubic feet. The EV also has considerably smaller towing and payload ratings, coming in at 2,000 and 1,550 pounds, respectively, versus the Ford's 13,500- and 2,440-pound figures.
That's hardly the whole story, though, as you can probably guess. For one thing, the Slate has a sizable frunk, adding another 7 cubic feet. Gas trucks lack frunks, since that's where the engine is located. More importantly, a better comparison point is other compact pickups, rather than something a landscaping contractor might park when they're about to redo your entire front lawn.
Viewed in that light, the Slate is very competitive. The base 2026 Ford Maverick for instance is largely on par, equipped for 1,500-pound payloads and 2,000 pounds of towing capacity. It actually has a shorter truck bed, measuring 4.5 feet. For the average person's supply runs at Home Depot, a Slate is the better choice. Especially since you're not going to be spending hundreds of dollars on inflated gas prices.
This sort of vehicle could be a godsend for drivers who just have the occasional heavy load, such as bikes, PEVs, furniture, moving boxes or camping equipment. People do often buy SUVs for that reason, yet the Slate is cheaper than many of them, and a truck bed is clearly easier to load and unload. Besides, you can configure the Slate as an SUV if you're determined to get that form factor.
The upgrade and battery efficiency problems
The thing that may kill the Slate's appeal for cargo and towing among some drivers is a problem with any electric truck, and that's a massive drop in range. Consider the Rivian R1T, which with the Adventure Quad-Motor Large Pack gets up to 328 miles. If you exploit its 11,000-pound maximum towing capacity, range drops 50 percent to about 164 miles. The Slate has a maximum range of 205 miles under good conditions, so realistically, you may be looking at 100 miles or less if you're towing at its 2,000-pound limit. If you fill up the bed with cargo instead, range could still drop by as much as 25 percent, if the F-150 Lightning is anything to go by.
Regardless, the Slate is also extremely barebones in its default configuration, as we mentioned earlier. Even an integrated speaker is a paid add-on, never mind things like lifting or dropping the suspension. To meet your exact needs, you'll almost certainly be spending over that $24,950 entry price. SUV startup packs can easily start north of $30,000, though thankfully, pickups tend to be cheaper.
We'll have to wait for post-launch testing to truly judge the Slate's hauling capacity. At the moment, all we can say for certain is that if you can deal with the range hit and jettisoned luxuries, the EV appears to go toe to toe with other compact pickups. If you can keep the price low, it may be worth it.

title_en: Mercedes-AMG’s first ground-up SUV is a 1,150hp electric beast
title_fa: Mercedes-AMG’s first ground-up SUV is a 1,150hp electric beast
excerpt_en: Earlier this year, Mercedes' AMG performance brand grabbed our attention with the GT four-door coupe, a souped-up sports sedan with three axial flux motors delivering over 1,150 horsepower. Well, now meet its beefier cousin, the 2028 Mercedes-AMG GT SUV, an equally powerful,...
excerpt_fa: Earlier this year, Mercedes' AMG performance brand grabbed our attention with the GT four-door coupe, a souped-up sports sedan with three axial flux motors delivering over 1,150 horsepower. Well, now meet its beefier cousin, the 2028 Mercedes-AMG GT SUV, an equally powerful,...
content_en:
Earlier this year, Mercedes’ AMG performance brand grabbed our attention with the GT four-door coupe, a souped-up sports sedan with three axial flux motors delivering over 1,150 horsepower. Well, now meet its beefier cousin, the 2028 Mercedes-AMG GT SUV, an equally powerful, ultra-fast-charging electric people-hauler.
Mercedes-AMG’s first ground-up SUV is a 1,150hp electric beast
It may even out-muscle the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric and Lucid Gravity.
It may even out-muscle the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric and Lucid Gravity.
The AMG GT SUV (say that five times fast) marks the first time in the performance brand’s 59-year history that it has developed a full-size SUV entirely in-house from the ground up. Scheduled to hit the US next summer, the new EV is built on Merc’s high-performance AMG.EA architecture to combine sports-car handling with full-size SUV suburban practicality.
It will be available in three trims — GT 53, GT 55, and the flagship GT 63 — with the top model delivering 1,153hp via the same three axial flux motors powering the four-door coupe. That beats the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric with Launch Control, which is sure to make for some awkward run-ins around Stuttgart.
Thanks to an 800-volt architecture, the SUV supports blistering-fast charging speeds up to 710kW on the 128kWh battery (GT 63 / GT 55) and 600kW on the 106kWh battery (GT 53). Drivers can charge 10–80 percent in 12 minutes or gain up to 450km (around 280 miles) of WLTP range in just 10 minutes. The 128kWh battery trims will have an estimated max range of 435 miles.
That battery, by the way? It utilizes F1-inspired technology with specialized NCMA cathodes, silicon-containing anodes, and cylindrical cells. An electrically nonconductive oil flows directly around each individual cell for uniform thermal management, enabling continuous high-power delivery and long battery life. Mercedes has quietly been on the vanguard of battery technology for a while now, with the AMG GT SUV just the latest example. The 710kW charging speed, in particular, could give Mercedes another edge over Porsche’s 320kW speeds.
For a full-size SUV, the AMG GT sounds like it could handle like a vehicle half its size. Mercedes-AMG replaced the traditional mechanical roll bars with a newly developed suspension that uses active hydraulic elements to eliminate pitch and roll during acceleration, heavy braking, and cornering. Combined with three-stage air springs and standard six-degree active rear-axle steering, it purports to balance track precision with long-distance comfort.
But just because it’s a beefy lad doesn’t mean it’ll tip the scales. The AMG GT 63 SUV weighs in at 5,941lbs, making it slightly lighter than the Lotus Eletre R (6,007lbs) and Lucid Gravity (6,100lbs), and nearly identical to the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric (5,960lbs).
Silence is golden — except to a performance brand’s EV engineering team. That means piping in recorded sounds of real AMGs — in this case, the legendary AMG V8 and six-cylinder engines — to preserve the “emotional” AMG identity. Mercedes is proud that it’s using real engine sounds over synthetic EV tones, though some may disagree. The system even simulates mechanical gear shifts with paddle controls, offers adjustable sound profiles, and integrates physical seat vibrations — so you can still feel like there’s a real engine under that hood instead of a 78-liter frunk. The so-called AMGFORCE Sport+ drive program is offered as standard across all three trims of the Mercedes-AMG GT SUV.
Inside, you’ll find the MB.OS platform on your 14-inch display, with an army of AI agents from ChatGPT, Microsoft, and Google at your disposal to boss around. Use them to set navigation, discover random locations, do web searches, tell bad jokes, or whatever else people use AI for in their cars. Merc’s own onboard AI system can handle the physical stuff, like adjusting HVAC, changing drive modes, or fiddling with the lighting — all through voice commands.
Beyond voice and navigation, the AMG GT SUV applies AI to high-performance track driving through something called the Predictive Performance Manager. Mercedes says the PPM uses track-mapping data to dynamically throttle or boost electric motor output depending on topography, conserving battery energy on downhill or technical winding sections so full power is available on steep inclines and long straights. That could also mean faster, more consistent overall lap times by eliminating battery overheating and power throttling during track driving — something an AMG lover would likely appreciate.
Mercedes didn’t release the official pricing yet, though we can expect something closer to its official launch.

That battery, by the way? It utilizes F1-inspired technology with specialized NCMA cathodes, silicon-containing anodes, and cylindrical cells. An electrically nonconductive oil flows directly around each individual cell for uniform thermal management, enabling continuous high-power delivery and long battery life. Mercedes has quietly been on the vanguard of battery technology for a while now, with the AMG GT SUV just the latest example. The 710kW charging speed, in particular, could give Mercedes another edge over Porsche’s 320kW speeds.
For a full-size SUV, the AMG GT sounds like it could handle like a vehicle half its size. Mercedes-AMG replaced the traditional mechanical roll bars with a newly developed suspension that uses active hydraulic elements to eliminate pitch and roll during acceleration, heavy braking, and cornering. Combined with three-stage air springs and standard six-degree active rear-axle steering, it purports to balance track precision with long-distance comfort.
But just because it’s a beefy lad doesn’t mean it’ll tip the scales. The AMG GT 63 SUV weighs in at 5,941lbs, making it slightly lighter than the Lotus Eletre R (6,007lbs) and Lucid Gravity (6,100lbs), and nearly identical to the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric (5,960lbs).
Silence is golden — except to a performance brand’s EV engineering team. That means piping in recorded sounds of real AMGs — in this case, the legendary AMG V8 and six-cylinder engines — to preserve the “emotional” AMG identity. Mercedes is proud that it’s using real engine sounds over synthetic EV tones, though some may disagree. The system even simulates mechanical gear shifts with paddle controls, offers adjustable sound profiles, and integrates physical seat vibrations — so you can still feel like there’s a real engine under that hood instead of a 78-liter frunk. The so-called AMGFORCE Sport+ drive program is offered as standard across all three trims of the Mercedes-AMG GT SUV.
Inside, you’ll find the MB.OS platform on your 14-inch display, with an army of AI agents from ChatGPT, Microsoft, and Google at your disposal to boss around. Use them to set navigation, discover random locations, do web searches, tell bad jokes, or whatever else people use AI for in their cars. Merc’s own onboard AI system can handle the physical stuff, like adjusting HVAC, changing drive modes, or fiddling with the lighting — all through voice commands.
Beyond voice and navigation, the AMG GT SUV applies AI to high-performance track driving through something called the Predictive Performance Manager. Mercedes says the PPM uses track-mapping data to dynamically throttle or boost electric motor output depending on topography, conserving battery energy on downhill or technical winding sections so full power is available on steep inclines and long straights. That could also mean faster, more consistent overall lap times by eliminating battery overheating and power throttling during track driving — something an AMG lover would likely appreciate.
Mercedes didn’t release the official pricing yet, though we can expect something closer to its official launch.

title_en: Elon Musk settles lawsuits over $1 million voter giveaway
title_fa: Elon Musk settles lawsuits over $1 million voter giveaway
excerpt_en: In 2024, Elon Musk promised to give away $1 million a day to a randomly selected registered voter in a swing state. That prompted legal challenges, raised questions about its legality, and drew lawsuits from two Arizona residents claiming the lottery was a fraud. Musk has now...
excerpt_fa: In 2024, Elon Musk promised to give away $1 million a day to a randomly selected registered voter in a swing state. That prompted legal challenges, raised questions about its legality, and drew lawsuits from two Arizona residents claiming the lottery was a fraud. Musk has now...
content_en:
In 2024, Elon Musk promised to give away $1 million a day to a randomly selected registered voter in a swing state. That prompted legal challenges, raised questions about its legality, and drew lawsuits from two Arizona residents claiming the lottery was a fraud. Musk has now agreed to settle the two lawsuits filed in Austin, Texas, though the details of the settlement have not been made public.
Elon Musk settles lawsuits over $1 million voter giveaway
Plaintiffs claiming Musk’s $1 million voter lottery was a fraud are settling for an undisclosed sum.
Plaintiffs claiming Musk’s $1 million voter lottery was a fraud are settling for an undisclosed sum.
The plaintiffs claim that when Musk announced the sweepstakes, he falsely claimed the prizes would be awarded randomly. Philadelphia’s District Attorney sued to stop the giveaway, claiming that Musk was running an illegal lottery. During a hearing, Chris Gober, a representative for Musk’s America PAC, told the judge that “The $1 million recipients are not chosen by chance … We know exactly who will be announced as the $1 million recipient today and tomorrow.”
That directly contradicted Musk’s claim that the drawings were random. The plaintiffs say they never would have signed the petition required to enter the giveaway if they had known it wasn’t random. They accused Musk and America PAC of using it as a ploy to obtain user data and said the petition “places no limitations on America PAC’s use of or sale of the personal data it collects, nor does it provide any additional information about the planned use of data.”

title_en: What does the yellow light on your Alexa device mean and how do you clear it?
title_fa: What does the yellow light on your Alexa device mean and how do you clear it?
excerpt_en: Don't panic if your Amazon Echo is flashing a yellow light. Here's what that color means, how to clear it and how to tweak your Alexa notification settings.
excerpt_fa: Don't panic if your Amazon Echo is flashing a yellow light. Here's what that color means, how to clear it and how to tweak your Alexa notification settings.
content_en:
What does the yellow light on your Alexa device mean and how do you clear it?
Here’s what your Echo's yellow light is trying to tell you and what to do about it.
Your Amazon Echo's light ring is a valuable information hub. And while most users are familiar with the recognizable blue ring, many don't realize that the light ring can display nine different color notifications, some of which are intended to grab your attention. If you see a flashing yellow ring around your Echo device, don't panic: a yellow light emanating in slow bursts every few seconds means that Alexa has a message or notification it would like to share with you.
Introduced in 2017, this notification system transforms your Echo into a proactive assistant, capable of alerting you to everything from breaking news and calendar reminders to notifying you when Amazon has shipped your latest package. It is also useful for taking advantage of some of Alexa's more advanced features, such as Alexa for Shopping's price-drop alert tool. Ultimately, customizing your Alexa notification settings is the key to maximizing your Echo's functionalities.
If your device begins flashing its yellow light, you can easily clear the issue by asking Alexa a question regarding your notifications or messages. For example, try "What notifications do I have?" or "What messages do I have?" From there, Alexa will recite the list of relevant notifications, which you can respond to as you see fit. You can also move through your notifications using simple phrases (such as "next" or "repeat").
Managing your notification settings
You can edit notification settings via the Alexa app on your phone or tablet. Tap the More symbol, which looks like three horizontal lines, and select Settings (the gear icon). From there, navigate to Notifications. In this section, you can toggle the features, services and apps you would like to enable or disable notifications for.
One setting to customize is how Alexa interacts with reminders. If the flashing yellow light is for a reminder you have missed, you can clear the notification by asking Alexa, "What are my reminders?" Then, you can issue a series of helpful commands, including asking Alexa to turn off, dismiss, snooze or reschedule your reminder. To change reminder notification settings, navigate to the Notifications section of your Alexa app. From there, select Reminders on this Device and toggle your Notifications on or off.
Another useful notification center is your Alexa Skills hub. Alexa Skills are voice-activated applications that expand Alexa's capabilities. The apps span a range of functions, including Health & Fitness, Productivity, Smart Home features, Sports, Education and even Trivia games. To edit your Alexa Skills notifications, open the Alexa app, then navigate to More > Skills & Games. From there, select Your Skills > Settings > Manage Account Permissions, toggle Notifications on or off and select Save Permissions.
You may also receive a notification if your Alexa-connected smart camera or doorbell detects a person, a package or a similar camera event. To manage these alerts, return to your Alexa app and select Devices. From there, select your connected camera and tap Device Settings. Next, toggle Person or Package Detection Announcements to your desired setting. Now, when your Alexa+ answers the doorbell, you'll have a yellow notification ring waiting for you.
A guide to your Echo's light scheme
Your Echo uses a range of lights to indicate its status. You are likely familiar with the iconic cyan light, which tells you Alexa is listening and glimmers whenever Alexa has heard and is processing a request. The cyan ring will also shimmer whenever your device receives a software update. A teal-blue light, on the other hand, signals that Alexa is waiting for you to issue a command. If you see the two shades of blue spinning around the outer ring, your device is likely starting up or restarting after a completed software update.
A red ring shows a key functionality is turned off. Appearing when you press the microphone on/off button, for instance, it tells users that the device's microphone is disconnected. To get rid of the light, simply press your microphone button again. For an Echo with a camera, a red light bar indicates that the device will not share your video.
If you see a bright orange light spinning around the outside edge of your Echo, the device is either in setup mode or trying to connect to the internet. A pulsing green light, meanwhile, means that you have an incoming call. Once you answer the call, the green ring will begin to spin. The effect is also used for active Drop In intercom sessions. A brief purple flash means that your device is in Do Not Disturb mode. During setup, it indicates Wi-Fi issues. Lastly, a white light shows the volume level whenever you adjust it.

title_en: Anbernic's RG DDS is almost double the price of the original Nintendo 3DS
title_fa: Anbernic's RG DDS is almost double the price of the original Nintendo 3DS
excerpt_en: The premium handheld is expected to start shipping in December.
excerpt_fa: The premium handheld is expected to start shipping in December.
content_en:
Anbernic's RG DDS is almost double the price of the original Nintendo 3DS
The premium handheld is expected to start shipping in December.
In creating a premium dual-screen handheld that's largely a callback to the Nintendo 3DS, Anbernic has made something that far surpasses the original in both price and power. Straying away from its reputation of churning out budget handhelds, Anbernic set its new RG DDS' price at $299.99, offering only a temporary preorder discount to $284.99.
To justify the cost, the RG DDS runs on a Snapdragon G2 Gen 2 that can emulate more than just 3DS titles. While we already knew the processor when Anbernic first teased its next clamshell device, the handheld maker fleshed out the rest of the specs, detailing two options between one with 8GB memory and 128GB of storage and an upgraded option with 12GB memory and 256GB of storage. However, both devices have a microSD card slot that can support up to 2TB of extra storage.
Anbernic said the RG DDS will use Android 16, allowing customers to take advantage of the many emulator apps out there. To round out the handheld, Anbernic included Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.4 compatibility, 1080p display output, a six-axis gyroscope sensor and a 3.5mm audio jack. As expected, there will be no glasses-free 3D graphics, as seen in the original 3DS, but the higher resolution displays might make up for it. As for the curious AI button that Anbernic revealed as part of the RG DDS' design, the company said it will offer game guides and strategies, real-time translation during gameplay and "more fun AI features."
Anbernic said the RG DDS will ship "gradually starting December 10, 2026." Confirming the colors teased in the video last week, the latest clamshell handheld will come in Glacier White, Basalt Black and Phantom Blue.

title_en: This Samsung Galaxy feature can protect you from untrustworthy apps
title_fa: This Samsung Galaxy feature can protect you from untrustworthy apps
excerpt_en: Samsung's Auto Blocker protects your Galaxy phone from security threats, but it does have drawbacks. Here's what it does and when you might want to turn it off.
excerpt_fa: Samsung's Auto Blocker protects your Galaxy phone from security threats, but it does have drawbacks. Here's what it does and when you might want to turn it off.
content_en:
This Samsung Galaxy feature can protect you from untrustworthy apps
Samsung's Auto Blocker keeps threats at bay, but it can also get in your way.
If you own a Samsung Galaxy phone running One UI 6.0 or later, you may have a built-in security feature called Auto Blocker working in the background without even realizing it. Enabled by default on devices that ship with One UI 6.1.1 or later, it filters out apps, USB commands and messages that could put your device at risk without you even having to lift a finger. For most people, that's a super useful layer of protection in a world where threats are extremely common and can come from apps, a public charging cable or images you get in a text.
But Auto Blocker isn't without its complications, especially for users who like to sideload apps, work with developer tools or install software from outside the Google Play Store or the Samsung Galaxy Store. Epic Games even filed a lawsuit against Samsung a couple of years ago, arguing that this very feature made downloading third-party apps unnecessarily difficult.
Understanding what Auto Blocker actually does and what it doesn't can help you make a smarter decision about whether to keep it on, turn it off or somewhere in between. Let's see what this feature does, how you can enable or disable it and what's the best thing to do.
What is Samsung Auto Blocker and what does it do?
Auto Blocker is a built-in security feature available on Galaxy devices using One UI 6 or higher. Its main job is to stop app installation from outside the Google Play Store or Samsung's Galaxy Store, efficiently closing off one of the most common ways malware ends up on a phone. It also takes things a step further and blocks malicious commands sent through a USB cable, which matters if you've ever charged your phone using a public cable. Beyond that, Auto Blocker filters images suspected of containing malicious code in messaging apps like Samsung Messages, Google Messages, Messenger, WhatsApp or Telegram.
For users who want even stronger protections, Samsung offers another mode called "Maximum restrictions," which adds extra safeguards, such as blocking device admin apps and work profiles, disabling 2G network connections, preventing auto-reconnection to unsecured Wi-Fi and stripping location data from shared photos. It's definitely a more aggressive setting, increasing security at the expense of convenience.
How to enable and disable Auto Blocker
Epic Games sued Google and Samsung back in 2024. The feature, they said, combined with existing Play Store and Galaxy Store flows, forced users to take over 20 steps just to download the Epic Games Store. The lawsuit was eventually dropped after Epic reached an agreement with Samsung, but the Auto Blocker stayed on.
If you need to sideload an app or run a developer tool, you can turn Auto Blocker off by going to Settings > Security and privacy > Auto Blocker and tapping the toggle. You'll need to authenticate before switching it off, which is a great feature that can protect you if someone gets their hands on your phone and tries to install some malware. The same path lets you turn it back on.
On phones running One UI 8.5 or later, you can also enable an option that automatically turns Auto Blocker back on 30 minutes after it's disabled. This lets you temporarily disable the protection to install an app without having to remember to reactivate it. You can find this extra toggle by tapping on the Auto Blocker feature in the menu.
Should you keep Auto Blocker enabled?
As you'd expect, Samsung recommends keeping Auto Blocker on, and for most users, that's sound advice. The feature is efficient in guarding against malicious apps, unauthorized USB access and tampered software updates; threats that are easy to overlook until something goes wrong.
The trade-offs are real, though, because Auto Blocker intentionally blocks APK installs from outside the Play Store and Galaxy Store, which affects anyone who relies on open-source apps or sideloaded tools. The most balanced approach is to leave Auto Blocker enabled by default and disable it only when you have a specific reason to install something from outside official app stores. Once you're done, you turn it back on, or, if you're running One UI 8.5 or later, you can have it automatically turn back on after 30 minutes.
If you're an advanced user who sideloads often, the auto re-enable option can feel like a nuisance. Just keep in mind that disabling Auto Blocker removes an additional layer of security. Other protections, including Google Play Protect, can still help guard against malicious apps, but it's important to verify the source of anything you install from outside official app stores. For people who want the opposite approach, Samsung's Maximum restrictions mode adds plenty of extra protections.

title_en: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
title_fa: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
excerpt_en: The biggest change about Ember's new mug is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature.
excerpt_fa: The biggest change about Ember's new mug is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature.
content_en:
With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3, the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip.
Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades.
The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click.
Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate.
It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app.
That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach.
If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings.
The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.)
The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149.
The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green.
Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2, which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out.
The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.

Enter Ember’s new Mug 3, the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip.
Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades.
The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click.
Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate.
It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app.
That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach.
If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings.
The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.)
The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149.
The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green.
Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2, which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out.
The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.

title_en: Why are some locations blurred out on Google Maps?
title_fa: Why are some locations blurred out on Google Maps?
excerpt_en: When using Google Maps, it isn't rare to see blurred locations. Why does this happen? The answer is simple, and it has everything to do with security.
excerpt_fa: When using Google Maps, it isn't rare to see blurred locations. Why does this happen? The answer is simple, and it has everything to do with security.
content_en:
Why are some locations blurred out on Google Maps?
Want more privacy? Opt in to blur your home on Googe Maps Street View.
We live in a world of permanent blur — at least on Street View in Google Maps, where locations once blurred cannot be unblurred. So why are some locations blurred on Google Maps, and what is it for?
Why is Google Maps Street View blurry?
Google can mask locations by blurring them on Street View. It does this in response to requests from government entities, digital privacy campaigners, and its own customers. It's all a matter of protecting the privacy of key people and places. The locations that tend to be blurred include:
- Military and highly secure government locations. You may also find that such secure locations are blurred or censored on other Google Earth products.
- The homes of high-net-worth individuals, celebrities, and VIPs.
- Privacy advocates and others who value digital privacy.
- Blurs applied in error, such as a mistaken address.
In some nations, including the Netherlands and Germany, people have a legal right to request that their home is blurred on these services, which is why so many properties there have been given that treatment.
The issue is that Google Street View provides detailed information on locations that can provide insight into property layout, value, and security protection. Police, criminals, open-source investigators, and journalists may potentially use Street View in their line of work. The blurring of this data on Street View reduces your digital footprint, which may protect you.
How to ask Google to blur your home
Google's Street View service already blurs people's faces and license plates by default using automated tools. If those tools fail to redact something, you can request removal of those items. You can also use the same process to request that your home be blurred.
- Open Google Maps and drag the pegman to the location you want to blur.
- Find the property in Street View when it opens.
- Click or tap the three dots (vertical ellipsis) in the top-left corner or tap the very small "Report a problem" text in the bottom right of the window.
- Adjust the view of the image to focus on the home, face or object you want to blur.
- Now choose what you want Google to blur.
- You'll be asked for your email address, which will be used to verify your request.
- You must complete a reCAPTCHA procedure.
- You may be asked to provide proof of tenancy or ownership of the property.
Can you turn off blurring in Google Maps Street View?
Google does not offer a way to undo the blurring of a location once it is applied. It's a permanent measure. That means that while blurring a property may help harden your security, it's not something you should do without thought. Not only does doing so prevent neighbors from exploring the entire street in Street View, but it also means potential future buyers and owners of the property will be unable to see the building.
There is also the counterintuitive argument that burglars studying an area for potential targets may see a blurred property as an attractive target, because that blurring suggests there may be something or someone valuable inside it.
How to blur locations on other mapping services
Wherever you stand on the blur or not to blur argument, it is important to recognize that blurring a property on Google Maps Street View does not blur that location on any other mapping services. To blur a property on Apple Maps, you should write to MapsImageCollection@apple.com including your name, address, and request details. Other mapping services, including Baidu Maps, Mapillary, and Karta View, may offer some form of street-level imaging service in your region. These may enable the blurring of specific locations on request. Microsoft removed its Streetside imagery from Bing Maps as part of its transition to Azure Maps.

title_en: Meta removes language that may have allowed it to scrape news sites
title_fa: Meta removes language that may have allowed it to scrape news sites
excerpt_en: After backlash, Meta is updating its terms again to remove language that suggested it could scrape content from sites, including news sites, to train its AI. Specifically, the following language no longer appears on the commercial terms page: … Meta may use any content from such...
excerpt_fa: After backlash, Meta is updating its terms again to remove language that suggested it could scrape content from sites, including news sites, to train its AI. Specifically, the following language no longer appears on the commercial terms page: … Meta may use any content from such...
content_en:
After backlash, Meta is updating its terms again to remove language that suggested it could scrape content from sites, including news sites, to train its AI. Specifically, the following language no longer appears on the commercial terms page:
Meta removes language that may have allowed it to scrape news sites
Language that experts say allowed the scraping of news sites to train its AI has been removed from Meta’s terms.
Language that experts say allowed the scraping of news sites to train its AI has been removed from Meta’s terms.
… Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.
Many, including Neiman Lab and James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, interpreted it as an attempt to give Meta the right to use content scraped from sites to train its AI products for free and supersede blocking instructions in a site’s robots.txt file.
Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, and spokesperson Daniel Roberts pushed back, saying that “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false.” Today’s update to its terms and a new statement go further, removing the controversial language entirely. Roberts said in a follow-up statement to The Verge this morning:
“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

title_en: Common problems with Amazon Alexa and how to fix them
title_fa: Common problems with Amazon Alexa and how to fix them
excerpt_en: Amazon Alexa is a very useful gadget to have at home, but it isn't exempt from having some issues. Fortunately, troubleshooting is easy as pie.
excerpt_fa: Amazon Alexa is a very useful gadget to have at home, but it isn't exempt from having some issues. Fortunately, troubleshooting is easy as pie.
content_en:
Common problems with Amazon Alexa and how to fix them
Some of the most common Alexa problems have very easy solutions.
Utilizing Alexa has become increasingly accessible since its release, with heaps of different Echo Dots and Shows to choose from alongside accessories like the Echo Auto and Echo Buds. You don't even need a physical device to access the service anymore with the new rollout of Alexa+. With so much proliferation, however, comes more and more room for things to go wrong.
At this point, it's entirely possible to design an entire smart home built on the back of Alexa. You can control your lights, sound systems, television, and security system all in one place, and set Routines to make them all work day-to-day with minimal effort. Of course, this doesn't come without downsides — aside from concerns surrounding the fact that Alexa is technically always listening, if you're reliant on Alexa, small common problems can have a big impact. Thankfully, they've also got easy solutions.
Fixes for common Alexa problems
If your Alexa doesn't understand you
If your Alexa doesn't seem to understand your voice, try setting up a Voice ID:
-
Open the Alexa app.
-
Select More, then Settings.
-
Select Account Management and select your profile.
-
Select Voice ID and follow the instructions.
You can also say, "Alexa, learn my voice" to the same effect.
If your Alexa is too talkative
If your Alexa's long-winded responses have become a bother, there are a couple of different methods you can try: Brief Mode and changing her personality type to Brief. The latter is one of several Alexa personality settings and will edit out things like filler statements while still speaking to you. The former is even more concise, often changing what would typically be a verbal response into a short sound cue to let you know you've been heard.
To turn on Brief personality:
-
Open the Alexa app.
-
Open Devices.
-
Select your device, then select Settings.
-
Select Alexa's Personality Style and choose Brief.
To turn on Brief Mode:
-
Open the Alexa app.
-
Select More, then Settings.
-
Select Voice Responses.
-
Turn Brief Mode on.
Both of these settings can also be enabled verbally by saying, "Alexa, enable Brief Mode" or "Alexa, change your personality style to Brief."
If your Alexa keeps waking to random words
If normal conversation keeps activating your Alexa, try changing your Wake Word to something less common:
-
Open the Alexa app.
-
Select Devices, then select your device.
-
Select Device Settings, then Wake Word.
-
Choose a new Wake Word and hit OK.
You can also say, "Alexa, change your Wake Word." Unfortunately, the Wake Word can't be customized and must be chosen from a list.
If Alexa is playing from the wrong speaker
If you have multiple Alexas and it's playing music or other sounds through the wrong one, it's worth placing your devices into Groups based on the room they're in. Then, you can say things like, "Alexa, play music in the bedroom," to ensure the right speaker. To set up Groups:
-
Open the Alexa app.
-
Select Devices.
-
At the top, where you can find Groups, select New Group, then tap Create a room or device group and follow the prompts to customize the Group.
Tips for a buggy Alexa
Sometimes, an Alexa can just be completely unresponsive. If your Alexa can't seem to hear you, it's first worthwhile to try to eliminate other loud noises that might be causing interference. If that doesn't work, make sure that your Alexa isn't muted by checking for a solid red light (a ring of light on speaker devices or a red bar with a mute icon on screen devices). To unmute the device, find the mute button, which is typically on the top or side of the device, and press it to unmute.
If muting wasn't the cause, the next best course of action is a simple restart, which can be done by unplugging the device for a few seconds, then plugging it back in — this solution applies to other issues like general lag or freezing, too. It's also possible the problem is related to a poor Wi-Fi connection, which could be solved by restarting your router via the same unplug method. Sometimes, though, bugginess is something that has a software root cause. It's always worth checking for a software update by saying, "Alexa, check for software updates." If there is one, the device will automatically update, hopefully solving the issue.

content_en:
It’s hard to overstate Jad Abumrad’s impact on the podcasting world. He created and hosted Dolly Parton’s America and Fela Kuti: Fear No Man, two Peabody Award-winning shows that offered unprecedented looks at the lives of two of the most important music icons of the last century.
Jad Abumrad loves a butterfly knife and a good springy pillow
The Radiolab creator and host of Dolly Parton’s America answers The Verge’s weekend questionnaire.
Jad Abumrad loves a butterfly knife and a good springy pillow
The Radiolab creator and host of Dolly Parton’s America answers The Verge’s weekend questionnaire.
Before that, though, he created Radiolab, an experimental NPR show that leaned heavily on creative sound design and eventually helped redefine what a podcast could be. In the early days of podcasting, shows were often just a couple of people talking at each other at a table (some still are), or lazily repackaged radio broadcasts. Radiolab instead told deeply reported stories in themed episodes with original music and cinematic sound effects that helped enhance the storytelling. And often, the sounds and music were created by Abumrad himself.
Abumrad retired from Radiolab in 2022, leaving it in the capable hands of Latif Nasser and Lulu Miller. But he’s been plenty busy since then, not only producing Fear No Man, but also composing for film, theater, and dance, and serving as a distinguished research professor at Vanderbilt University.
Despite his intimidating resume, however, he’s a man of simple pleasures who collects an ungodly amount of audio plug-ins and loves the satisfying clack of a butterfly knife.
What is your most indispensable tool?
My pillow. I need a flat, springy pillow, and I don’t understand this new hotel / airbnb trend towards giant fluffy pillows that wreck your neck for a week (I’m that age). So, a good travel pillow. In terms of digital tools: it’s rare to say you love a calendar app, but I truly love Fantastical. It takes the most annoying task in the world — scheduling a meeting with many busy people — and makes it actually fun. In terms of digital audio tools: I am addicted to audio plugins and have a thousand too many, but the one I come back to over and over is a little granular synthesis app called Granite. It’s 15 years old at this point, but it’s just so musical. I’ve used it to score dozens of OG Radiolab pieces.
Which is the most underappreciated?
I think indoor plumbing is wildly underappreciated. I have a whole talk I give about the miracle of indoor plumbing.
What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?
Alfred. It’s a super lightweight do-everything replacement for Apple’s built-in Spotlight. Like Raycast but without the annoying AI features.
What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?
I wish I could eliminate all the buzzes and dings. In fact, I wish there were a button that could turn my smartphone into a very dumb phone, because I only need it to be smart a few minutes a day.
What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?
My tab bar is boring and functional: NYT, Ground.News, the Vanderbilt Library resource page (which links to Nexis and all the journals), ESPN.
How many tabs do you have open right now?
14, but today has been a big research day.
Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)?
I use Instagram sometimes. I used to be active on Twitter and had a decent following, pre-Elon, but then they changed the login process, and I got locked out. I never could get back in and stopped wanting to.
What is your happy place online?
Bandcamp, Andrew Huang’s YouTube channel.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
A tie between my Motorola flip phone from 1997 and a butterfly knife I saved up for a decade earlier. Snapping open and shut the phone satisfied some deep, restless urge, and the same was true for the rotational flourish of the wrist involved in opening and closing the knife.
Which was the most disappointing?
Muse brainwave headset.
What game do you have the fondest memories of?
Around the same time as the butterfly knife, I used to save up quarters all week and then run to the local Kroger and play Donkey Kong. I was never good. But I do have a distinct memory of one time getting to a new level, barrels flying everywhere. I remember the depths of that adrenaline rush.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
People walking their dogs while looking at their phones. Maddening.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
The soundtrack to Birth. Alexandre Desplat is a shape-shifting genius, and that movie, in addition to being peculiar and amazing, has one of the most haunting scores ever.
What creation are you most proud of?

Jad Abumrad loves a butterfly knife and a good springy pillow

Jad Abumrad loves a butterfly knife and a good springy pillow
The Radiolab creator and host of Dolly Parton’s America answers The Verge’s weekend questionnaire.
Before that, though, he created Radiolab, an experimental NPR show that leaned heavily on creative sound design and eventually helped redefine what a podcast could be. In the early days of podcasting, shows were often just a couple of people talking at each other at a table (some still are), or lazily repackaged radio broadcasts. Radiolab instead told deeply reported stories in themed episodes with original music and cinematic sound effects that helped enhance the storytelling. And often, the sounds and music were created by Abumrad himself.
Abumrad retired from Radiolab in 2022, leaving it in the capable hands of Latif Nasser and Lulu Miller. But he’s been plenty busy since then, not only producing Fear No Man, but also composing for film, theater, and dance, and serving as a distinguished research professor at Vanderbilt University.
Despite his intimidating resume, however, he’s a man of simple pleasures who collects an ungodly amount of audio plug-ins and loves the satisfying clack of a butterfly knife.
What is your most indispensable tool?
My pillow. I need a flat, springy pillow, and I don’t understand this new hotel / airbnb trend towards giant fluffy pillows that wreck your neck for a week (I’m that age). So, a good travel pillow. In terms of digital tools: it’s rare to say you love a calendar app, but I truly love Fantastical. It takes the most annoying task in the world — scheduling a meeting with many busy people — and makes it actually fun. In terms of digital audio tools: I am addicted to audio plugins and have a thousand too many, but the one I come back to over and over is a little granular synthesis app called Granite. It’s 15 years old at this point, but it’s just so musical. I’ve used it to score dozens of OG Radiolab pieces.

I think indoor plumbing is wildly underappreciated. I have a whole talk I give about the miracle of indoor plumbing.

title_en: Should you have both Ethernet and Wi-Fi for your home?
title_fa: Should you have both Ethernet and Wi-Fi for your home?
excerpt_en: Ethernet will keep your devices connecting online in record time, while Wi-Fi keeps them untethered. But how well can they both work together?
excerpt_fa: Ethernet will keep your devices connecting online in record time, while Wi-Fi keeps them untethered. But how well can they both work together?
content_en:
Should you have both Ethernet and Wi-Fi for your home?
Wi-Fi and Ethernet work together for a great blend of convenience and reliability.
Even though so many devices use wireless connections, Ethernet still has a place in your home network. The latest Wi-Fi standards make big improvements, but a wireless connection often can't compete with a cable. You probably don't mind the speed sacrifice when you're scrolling Instagram on your phone in bed, but it makes a difference when downloading game updates or uploading large files.
Ethernet might fall short compared to Wi-Fi depending on your internet service provider (ISP) and hardware. But a general guideline is that Wi-Fi is fine when convenience is most important, while Ethernet is superior for any device where you need full speed and top reliability. Having a setup equipped for both makes for a healthy home network where everyone is happy.
Use Wi-Fi for devices where convenience matters most
If you've done a home internet speed test, you've likely noticed that the speeds you get on Wi-Fi don't match what you pay your ISP for. Wireless setups are typically slower than wired ones for several reasons. Wi-Fi signals suffer from overhead in managing their connections, especially when many devices are sharing the limited bandwidth at once. They also degrade as they travel, and they have trouble passing through thick obstacles like metal walls or concrete. Other wireless signals from devices like microwaves and baby monitors can interfere with older 2.4GHz Wi-Fi signals, and nearby Wi-Fi networks can cause interference, too.
Despite all this, Wi-Fi still has a place. It wouldn't be feasible to connect all your smart home devices (appliances, cameras, plugs, and more) to your router with a cable, especially since many of them lack Ethernet ports. Plus, most of what these devices do — along with what most people do on phones, tablets, and even laptops — works perfectly fine with Wi-Fi's limitations. Unless you have a terrible router or extremely low internet speeds, you're not going to notice slightly higher latency or slower downloads while watching YouTube.
If you just want to get a device online, especially if it moves around the house regularly, connect it to Wi-Fi. Barring any compatibility issues with Wi-Fi security standards or wireless bands, it should work just fine. And if you want uniform coverage across your home, the best Mesh Wi-Fi systems can help with that, especially if you're forced to put your router behind thick walls.
Understanding Wi-Fi connection standards
Not all wireless connections are exactly the same. For wireless, the two most important factors are whether it's dual-band or tri-band and what generations of Wi-Fi your router and devices support. For a long time, Wi-Fi ran over two bands: 2.4GHz and 5GHz. The 2.4GHz band is the oldest; it reaches far but offers slower speeds, and it's more susceptible to interference. Meanwhile, the 5GHz band doesn't go as far, but it's faster and less interference-prone. The latest standards add the 6GHz band, which supports even faster speeds but has the lowest effective range. Not all devices work with 6GHz connections, but those that do experience much less interference.
The Wi-Fi generation of your router affects which bands it broadcasts on. Wi-Fi 5 started rolling out in 2013, so it's time to replace your router if you're still using one from then. Wi-Fi 6 arrived in 2020-2021 alongside Wi-Fi 6E. These are identical, except that Wi-Fi 6E supports the 6GHz band. And the latest, Wi-Fi 7, uses the 6GHz band in addition to other speed and performance improvements.
A dual-band router operates at both 2.4GHz and 5GHz. Depending on the generation, a "tri-band" router either means two 5GHz bands (Wi-Fi 6 devices) or 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz (Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 routers). Some high-end routers are quad-band, offering two 5GHz bands alongside 6GHz. Having a second 5GHz band provides a dedicated line for mesh network nodes to communicate with each other without affecting your devices on the other band. Without that, there's a higher chance of congestion. If you're reliant on Wi-Fi, that 6GHz band will make a difference for nearby devices, but check to make sure yours are compatible. For example, the PS5 Pro is the only PS5 model compatible with 6GHz Wi-Fi.
Wire with Ethernet for maximum performance
Ethernet sidesteps most of Wi-Fi's issues. It's a direct connection that doesn't suffer from interference in the air, meaning you'll see lower latency (ping) and speeds closer to what comes into your house from your ISP. Ethernet is full-duplex, which means it can send and receive information at the same time. In contrast, Wi-Fi is half-duplex, meaning it can only send or receive data at a given moment. If you use a desktop (or laptop) PC for network-heavy work, you'll appreciate an Ethernet connection. Video calls will be more stable, cloud storage will sync your files faster, downloads will be quicker, and everything should feel a bit snappier.
Wired connections also make a big difference in gaming. While you might think that fast speeds are crucial for online games, low latency is what's most important. With high ping, what you see on the screen is delayed from what's happening on the game's server. You're more likely to have problems here when Wi-Fi is dropping packets, suffering from interference, or cutting out entirely.
Wired connections can still be inconvenient, especially in larger homes where longer cables are needed to connect to routers. But there are ways to use Ethernet without running cables. And if you're out of Ethernet ports on your router, a network switch is an affordable, simple way to add more.

content_en:
Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.
SpaceX’s ambitious, expensive gamble to replace AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
Cell service isn’t rocket ships or flying cars, but it could be a booming business for SpaceX.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
Combined with news that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-gen Starlink satellites and the company’s previous agreement to purchase close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum last year, it’s now clear SpaceX is serious about competing with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.
I’ve covered the telecom business for a long time, and I’ve always known that these companies can say they want to do something until they run into the harsh reality of how expensive it is to actually do it. The telecom graveyard of pivots, bad ideas, and failed acquisitions is vast.
Walt has been closely monitoring SpaceX’s acquisition, and he’s correctly predicted that the company was headed in this direction for months now. So I wanted to dig into whether SpaceX can pull this off, why Walt thinks the existing telecom giants have really fumbled their response to SpaceX’s growing threat, and what happens when Elon Musk’s rocket company jumps headfirst into a business everyone loves to hate.
Okay: LightShed Partners’ Walter Piecyk on SpaceX’s plan to expand into mobile. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Walter Piecyk, you’re a partner and a tech, media, and telecom analyst at LightShed Partners. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks for having me. I’m looking forward to it.
I’m excited to talk to you. I feel like we’ve been tweeting or posting around each other for many, many years, but I’m a telecom nerd at heart. I’ve been covering the space for ages. SpaceX is going to make a big splash. It’s going to be the fourth major mobile carrier in the United States and maybe the world. It bought some spectrum to do it.
It’s EchoStar spectrum by way of private equity. It is at once very simple and also very complicated. Give us the state of the state. SpaceX bought 800 Mhz spectrum for $8 billion. They spent nearly $20 billion already on separate EchoStar spectrum. What is SpaceX trying to do here?
It’s definitely complicated, but maybe less complicated than trying to figure out how to put a data center out in space and making that work. Or something on the moon. But they don’t typically want to own spectrum and spend for spectrum. If you think about how Starlink was built, satellite companies don’t typically pay for spectrum. And then as the business evolved and as they saw the opportunity in telecom, they purchased some spectrum initially from EchoStar.
The feedback they got from investors at that time was very positive and they said, “Wait a minute, you should do more here.” This is a trillion-dollar enterprise value business in the US alone. Obviously they have global aspirations both for Starlink as well as what they’re doing with this mobile telephone service. So they bought more. They went back to EchoStar. That’s a key thing to pay attention to, in that they bought some spectrum and then they went back and bought some more.
Because with a lot of things that Elon Musk does, he learns as he goes. He bought the spectrum, got feedback, talked to people in telecom, and bought some more spectrum. Then we didn’t hear from them for a while. Now, you have this thing that happened last week where they bought some more spectrum, and I can go through the history of it if you care, but it’s long, wonky telecom stuff. This was originally the Nextel spectrum, if you remember that company.
I do. Actually, I do want you to go through the history because I think the telecom business is best understood as a bunch of lobbyists trying to make everything more complicated than it should be. Yes, spectrum auctions are complicated and what spectrum is good for what is deeply tied to the physics of the radio spectrum and all that.
But here it’s the 800 MHz spectrum from the Nextel service, the old push-to-talk, walkie-talkie service that Sprint had to divest as part of the deal to get sold to T-Mobile. They’ve been trying to sell it for ages. They sold it to this company, Grain Management. They’ve been sitting on it, and when Starlink showed up, Elon bought it. Nobody else wanted it. What did he see in the spectrum that no one else did?
When you realize that you need to build a terrestrial network to support what you’re doing with satellites, because satellites work fine if you’ve got your dish on the top of your house and you’re getting your broadband, but when you’re trying to connect with a phone that doesn’t have the same type of power or you’re going inside a home, you’re going to need better coverage.
Sirius Satellite also has supplementary towers. There are not that many of them, but sometimes when you get out of Sirius coverage, you will connect to a tower. When they bought that EchoStar spectrum and then got FCC approval, and if you looked into those details of that FCC approval and what was required, you would see that they can’t do this by satellites alone. There had to be terrestrial.
Then SpaceX, as Elon is wont to do, tries to send some diversions like, “We’re going to do Femtocell, we’re not going to do macrocell, this, that, and the other thing.” But they realized that they were going to build a terrestrial...

Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.
OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.
In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak, suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them.
Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup, raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.”
Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August. Amazon has since filed an amended complaint.
Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems
This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon, which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok, Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are.
“Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge. “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.”
Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents.
The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment.
Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.”
The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products.
While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.”

content_en:
After Apple courageously removed the headphone jack from the iPhone in 2016, most people switched to Bluetooth earbuds and never looked back. But their wired counterparts have stuck around, and their sales even went up this year after five years of decline.
Bose’s new wired earbuds are simple in the best way
Wired earbuds are making a small comeback, and Bose is capitalizing on it — with ANC this time.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Part of the resurgence can be tied to the fact that they’re cool now with younger generations — following the revival of tape decks and vinyl. Celebrities have been spotted wearing them, and there’s even an Instagram account that follows the trend. Wired earbuds have real benefits. They don’t need a battery, so they’ll last longer than wireless ones that eventually die, and it’s a lot harder to lose a wired pair with a long cable than a single earbud.
Now, after more than a decade, Bose has returned to the wired world, but the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are no throwbacks.
The Good
- One of the few sets of wired earbuds with ANC
- Comfortable and secure fit
- High-res audio
- Simple to use
The Bad
- Call quality isn’t great
- Wind noise is distracting
The $99 Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds connect over USB-C, so they don’t need an extra dongle to work with current phones. That’s also how they can offer ANC. Because the 3.5mm or 4.4mm analog audio connector doesn’t provide enough power for active noise cancellation, most wired earbuds, from cheap off-brands to wildly expensive audiophile in-ear monitors, rely on passive isolation only. Bose’s last attempt at wired in-ears with ANC, 2013’s QuietComfort 20, had a 3.5mm jack, and their ANC relied on a rechargeable battery in the cable. The new Bose earbuds don’t need the battery pack; they can get the minimal power they need for ANC from the USB-C port.
There are a few other USB-C wired headphones with active noise cancellation, but not many. There’s also the $30 Belkin SoundForm ANC Wired Earbuds, which reportedly have weak noise canceling, and Audio-Technica released a pair in Asia earlier this year.
The best part of the Bose earbuds, or any wired earbuds, is that they’re simple. No need to worry about pairing them, no need to charge them, and no need to fiddle with an app. Plug them into the USB-C port on a phone or computer and they just work.
While the noise canceling performance doesn’t measure up to Bose’s Bluetooth earbuds (the wired earbuds have two mics per side, while the QuietComfort Earbuds have three), it’s still solid for the price. It does a great job blocking low-frequency sounds like air conditioners and low truck rumbles, but has difficulty muting conversation (with ANC on, I can’t hear our air conditioner at all, but can make out every word of my wife’s phone conversation as I write this). There’s a slight high-end hiss when the noise canceling is active, but it’s only noticeable when they aren’t playing any sound.
And they sound great. Vocals are clear and bright, and bass is punchy without overwhelming other instruments. I wouldn’t mind being able to cut down the high-end brightness a bit (mainly to tame cymbal ringing), but since these don’t use an app there are no EQ options. The wired connection allows for low latency, so there’s no worry about sound and video lining up, and they support high-res audio at 24-bit/48kHz. I went back and forth between CD quality (16-bit/44.1kHz) and high-res streams of the new release of The Beatles’ Rubber Soul on Qobuz, and the high-res versions sounded a bit more open and spacious. It’s not an enormous difference, but I’d listen to the high-res version on the Bose over the CD-level stream any day.
The in-line remote has three buttons that control volume, playback, and noise-canceling mode selection. They respond quickly when pressed and have a nice rubberized texture. The headphones come with three ear tip sizes and two sets of wings to find a good fit (you don’t even need to use the wings if you find them uncomfortable). I was easily able to find a comfortable combination and they stayed securely in my ears for hours. The earbuds are also IPX4 rated if there’s a light rain while you’re out or you want to use them on a run.
Even with the benefits of wired earbuds, though, nostalgia can’t wipe away the frustrations. If you don’t run the 4.2-foot cable under your shirt, or coil up the excess in your jacket pocket, it catches on everything. In my short time with the Bose, the cable caught on the handle of a kitchen drawer, the edge of my keyboard, the zipper of my sweatshirt, the strap of a bag I was carrying, my pocket (when I accidentally stuffed too much of the excess in with my phone), and even the hand of a stranger who got too close to me in line at Starbucks.
And as with any wired earbuds, there’s cable noise, as vibrations from rubbing or bumping against something travel up the cable to be heard in the earbuds. Although I will say the cable insulation is enough to minimize the effect better than cheap (and older) options.
The Bose struggle with wind. The microphones for noise canceling or transparency mode pick up the wind noise, and it’s distracting — with ANC on, it cuts out the low-end whoosh decently, but the high end is still incredibly present. I found turning it off was best when it was windy outside, although that meant compromising on the noise canceling.
Call quality also isn’t the best. The microphone is on the in-line remote, and it picks up a good amount of ambient sound during calls. If you regularly make calls while walking busy streets, these aren’t the earbuds for you.
I’m not ready to go back to 2016 and convert back to wired earbuds. In most situations, the benefits of wireless earbuds outweigh those of wired ones, and I don’t see that changing for me. But for the ease of use, convenience of a USB-C connection, lack of lag, high-res capability, sound quality,...

title_fa: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
