title_en: Trump ballroom's biggest donors were overwelmingly tech and telecom companies
title_fa: Trump ballroom's biggest donors were overwelmingly tech and telecom companies
excerpt_en: Not that anyone's terribly surprised.
excerpt_fa: Not that anyone's terribly surprised.
content_en:
Trump ballroom's biggest donors were overwelmingly tech and telecom companies
Records also show that taxpayers are footing some of the bill.
The Washington Post has obtained a list of all of the major donors to President Trump's ballroom project thingamajig. The big reveal? The tech, telecom and crypto industries are the primary benefactors here, donating over $183 million for the audacious ballroom that nobody wants or asked for.
The biggest donors are NVIDIA and Apple, who each committed $25 million. The same goes for billionaire Charles Ergen, the co-founder of Dish Network. NVIDIA and Dish have both benefited significantly from Trump policies during this second term. As for Apple, it has been scrambling to curry favor with Trump so as to avoid some of those endless tariffs.
Exclusive: A list reveals all the major donors to President Trump's White House ballroom, including previously undisclosed contributors who have benefited from regulatory decisions, government contracts and, in one case, a pardon for a family member. https://t.co/y3ivMy1NKk
— The Washington Post (@washingtonpost) October 15, 2026
Nearly every other major tech company has also donated millions each to the project, including Microsoft, Meta, Palantir, Google, Amazon and Cisco, among others. This isn't exactly surprising, given that most of these companies were also heavily involved with funding the president's inauguration in 2025.
Republican megadonor Sheldon Adelson also gave $25 million and companies like Blackrock, Lockheed Martin, Gemini and Coinbase gave millions. There's also $77 million in funds unaccounted for, as ballroom donations aren't subject to public disclosure or campaign finance rules. It could be anyone or any entity from anywhere. This money is funneled to a "nonprofit" that the president directly controls, just how the constitution envisioned it.
Absent from this list of donors? President Trump. He has repeatedly vowed to help pay for the project, once saying "it's being paid for a hundred percent by me and some friends of mine." There's no money trail here with his name on it.
However, we'll be spending some of our cents to turn the now-demolished East Wing into a gaudy ballroom for the world's richest people to dance inside of. The Washington Post has also found American taxpayers could end up paying for around half of this thing when all is said and done. This is especially worrisome, given that the expected budget for the ballroom recently shot up to $600 million.
This being a Trump project, there are even more troubling potential connections between the President and some of these donors. Joseph Popolo Jr. donated $1 million to the ballroom just after being chosen as the ambassador to the Netherlands. He did not report this donation. Trump cabinet member Kelly Loeffler and her husband promised $5 million. Brandon Lutnick gave stock worth more than $2.5 million. That's the son of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
Finally, there's Isabela Herrera, who donated $2.5 million. This is the daughter of international banker Herrera Velutini, who was indicted by the Justice Department on bribery charges and pleaded guilty. His daughter made the first payment installment of $835,000 in October, 2025 and her father was pardoned by the president in January.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle expressed frustration that this list of donors was published and vowed that the administration will "relentlessly pursue those responsible for this cowardly leak while continuing to protect all those who give." He also said that reporters are just looking for "fake conflicts of interest."

title_en: Volvo makes a bigger bet on Nvidia for hands-free automated driving
title_fa: Volvo makes a bigger bet on Nvidia for hands-free automated driving
excerpt_en: Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia that will extend beyond its battery electric vehicles.
excerpt_fa: Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia that will extend beyond its battery electric vehicles.
content_en:
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. The companies announced on Thursday that Volvo will use three pieces of Nvidia hardware and software in its future vehicles to provide an automated driving system that can navigate urban streets and highways.
Under the expanded partnership, Volvo will combine its vehicle safety systems and engineering with Nvidia’s Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Alpamayo driving software stack, and Halos safety evaluation layer.
The Alpamayo stack is redundant and diverse, according to Ali Kani, who heads up Nvidia’s automotive division. It combines Alpamayo, a family of AI models, datasets, and simulation and development tools used to build autonomous-driving software, with classical software that uses machine learning and camera and radar perception, he said.
“The point is we run these two stacks at the same time, and we have multimodal sensors in our philosophy because it’s a safer product that way,” Kani said, adding that the open source Alpamayo software has now been downloaded by more than 650,000 developers.
Volvo didn’t reveal the value of the partnership or which vehicle model would be the first to use this new Nvidia tech stack. But Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo’s head of software development, hinted at the scale of the deal and how it represents the automaker’s evolution toward developing a full-tech stack designed for its electric vehicles as well as its plug-in hybrids and gas-powered vehicles.
“Automakers used to be very much like car-line-based development and working with various suppliers, etc. and we have completely changed and migrated into being a full-tech stack company,” Bakkenes said, adding that Volvo will start this partnership with a brand new vehicle that “will come in the not-too-near future.”
He said the first vehicle with this new Nvidia tech stack will debut within the decade, and “then of course the technology can go beyond that.”
While Volvo’s relationship with Nvidia isn’t new, the expanded partnership represents the automaker’s effort to bring the latest automated driving software to all of its vehicles — not just its EVs.
All of Volvo’s battery-electric vehicles use Nvidia’s Orin computer chip, which processes information from cameras, radar, and other sensors to help a vehicle understand its surroundings and make driving decisions.
“What we’re going to do in the future is actually standardize more on Hyperion — also from a sensor set perspective — to really open up the stack for the wider partnership with Nvidia,” Bakkenes said.

title_en: Meta built a huge open-weight AI model for Macs, but you'll need 1TB of RAM to run it
title_fa: Meta built a huge open-weight AI model for Macs, but you'll need 1TB of RAM to run it
excerpt_en: Muse Spark Open is "the most capable US open-weight model to date," the company says.
excerpt_fa: Muse Spark Open is "the most capable US open-weight model to date," the company says.
content_en:
Meta built a huge open-weight AI model for Macs, but you'll need 1TB of RAM to run it
Muse Spark Open is "the most capable US open-weight model to date," the company says.
In case there was still any doubt about Meta's commitment to open models, the company is open-sourcing Muse Spark with a new open-weight model called Muse Spark Open. The 800-billion parameter model was optimized for Apple Silicon, but you'll need a staggering 1TB of RAM to run it locally.
Meta, which has said it believes the US should not allow Chinese labs to lead on open-source AI, calls Muse Spark Open "the most capable US open-weight model to date." Benchmarks released by the company suggest Meta's model outperforms two leading Chinese models, GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3, on agentic tasks and visual reasoning.
It's also the first model optimized to run locally on Apple's M5 Ultra-equipped Mac Studio machines. "Apple's unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model," Meta explains. "The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory."
Muse Spark Open — weights releasing today — runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple. pic.twitter.com/U2wJNrKBOg
— Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) October 15, 2026
Apple still hasn't announced specific pricing or a ship date for the 512GB Mac Studio — just that it will be available in "late October" — any setup that can run Muse Spark Open will require a hefty investment. Muse Spark Open can also run on four 256GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios, which will cost roughly $38,000. That amount of compute is pretty squarely out of reach for the typical vibe coder. But if you're a larger organization that's been burning through your token budget, investing in a few Mac Studios might seem like a pretty good deal, provided Meta's model performs as well as the company suggests.
Muse Spark Open is available to download now from Hugging Face.

title_en: SK Hynix bargains for chip equipment exports to its China facility in return for building a factory in US
title_fa: SK Hynix bargains for chip equipment exports to its China facility in return for building a factory in US
excerpt_en: SK Hynix’s Solidigm is reportedly seeking U.S. approval to send more chipmaking equipment to China as it weighs building a new NAND chip factory in America.
excerpt_fa: SK Hynix’s Solidigm is reportedly seeking U.S. approval to send more chipmaking equipment to China as it weighs building a new NAND chip factory in America.
content_en:
SK Hynix appears to be navigating choppy U.S.-China chipmaking waters. The company’s flash memory unit, Solidigm, is seeking U.S. approval to send American chipmaking equipment to its factory in Dalian, China, as a condition to continue building a semiconductor factory in the U.S., Reuters reported, citing anonymous sources.
Solidigm has been reportedly chalking up plans to build a NAND flash memory chip factory in the U.S. and is considering upstate New York as a potential location for the facility.
NAND flash chips are primarily used in solid-state storage drives, which are employed in everything from laptops and smartphones to AI data centers. But the global component shortage, thanks to skyrocketing demand for AI data centers, has driven up prices for everything that goes into data centers, including high-speed RAM chips and SSDs. Research firm TrendForce expects NAND prices to rise 15% to 20% in the fourth quarter.
Reuters cited its sources as saying that Solidigm wants to install more chipmaking equipment in spare space at SK Hynix’s Dalian factory in China to boost NAND chip production.
SK Hynix told TechCrunch it is not seeking to expand capacity at its Dalian Mod B facility, which was completed in 2023. The chip giant added that the equipment installation is being carried out in consultation with and under authorization from the U.S. government.
Washington first imposed sweeping restrictions on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment exports to China in October 2022, citing national security concerns, and further tightened the rules in 2023. Then in September 2025, the Trump administration revoked special export exemptions for certain SK Hynix, Samsung, and Intel facilities in China. The U.S. has since granted an annual license to Samsung and SK Hynix for sending chipmaking equipment to their plants in China.
The U.S. has also been pushing foreign chipmakers to build and expand their manufacturing facilities in America. In July, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said he wanted Samsung and SK Hynix to build chip plants in the country and that he was in talks with both companies.
Solidigm is said to be preparing for a 2027 U.S. IPO that could raise around $10 billion and value it at up to $100 billion.

title_en: GuliKit TT Max review: The granddaddy of Switch 2 controllers
title_fa: GuliKit TT Max review: The granddaddy of Switch 2 controllers
excerpt_en: This is the Switch 2 gamepad for big hands.
excerpt_fa: This is the Switch 2 gamepad for big hands.
content_en:
GuliKit TT Max review: The granddaddy of Switch 2 controllers
This is the Switch 2 gamepad for big hands.
The TT Max from GuliKit is the heftiest Switch 2 controller in town. Wider, thicker and heavier than Nintendo's Pro Controller or 8BitDo's Ultimate 2, the TT Max feels like it was designed to make PC, Xbox and PlayStation fans feel at home on Switch 2. With aligned and adjustable TMR thumbsticks, four removable back paddles, a customizable floating D-pad, multiplatform support and other quality features, the TT Max is a versatile gamepad for serious play on the Switch 2 and beyond.
In the world of controllers generally, the TT Max is a standard size and fairly lightweight, but compared with Switch 2 gamepads, it's a beast. In my admittedly small hands, it sits more like an Xbox pad than a Nintendo Pro Controller, though it has aligned joysticks like a DualSense. (Dr. Frankenstein would be proud.) The metal rear paddles, which are attached out of the box, are raised above the grips like slim butterfly wings and they press in with a satisfying click. They make the controller feel even bigger than its chassis, for better or worse.
The entire gamepad hits fidget-toy-levels of fulfillment: Its triggers flare upward and are roughly textured at the tips, and there's a switch to swap between an ultra-smooth Hall effect pull and a digital click. The controller's face is matte plastic while its rear grips are heavily textured like the triggers, and the bumpers are nice and wide. The floating circular D-pad can be set to a 4-way or 8-way mode, and the TMR thumbsticks are super precise, with a slick glide and adjustable stepless tension. The TT Max comes with an extra D-pad and a stick kit providing two additional heights, each featuring silicone caps with low-profile edges.

When paired with the Switch 2, the controller's default mode is HD vibration. While this offers pinpoint haptics and a lovely all-over rumble, it tends to make a grinding noise that's noticeable even over the on-screen frenzy of Resident Evil Requiem. Perhaps unsurprisingly, rotary mode is even louder and crunchier. GuliKit's proprietary maglev haptic mode, the default for PC play, is the quietest and least mechanical-sounding of the bunch, and it's my personal favorite. Note that this is all based on the standard intensity setting, and there's one softer and one stronger, so you should be able to find something that works for your palms and ears equally.
One of the most luxurious features that a Switch 2 controller can have is the ability to wake up the console, and here, the TT Max has you covered. It pairs easily to the Switch 2 and will reliably wake up the console with a press of the home button, and the controller's in-box instructions are easy to follow all around. It doesn't feature a player indicator on the chassis, but it has lights to signal pairing mode and battery life between the bumpers. I haven't encountered any issues with the TT Max's lifespan, since it easily charges via a USB-C port; GuliKit says it can last up to 26 hours with the RGBs off, or 14 hours with the lights on low.
I was surprised to see that the TT Max also comes with a simple hard case perfectly molded to the controller's contours, providing protection while traveling or living with perpetually sticky kids, roommates, cats, bees, etc. The case is nothing special, but it's really nice to have.
To neatly recap, here are all of the accessories included in the TT Max's box:
- Three analog stick pairs of varying heights, one pair attached
- PC-layout keycaps
- Keycap puller
- Tension adjustment tool
- Four metal paddles, attached to the rear grips
- Two D-pads, one attached
- Hyperlink 2 wireless USB adapter
- USB-C to USB charging cable
- Protective case
- User manual (that's actually useful)
All of that comes with a sturdy, versatile and reliable gamepad that works across Switch, Switch 2, PC, Android and iOS, and still costs $20 less than the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller. GuliKit's TT Max is $70, placing it near the middle of the pack when it comes to Switch 2 controller pricing.
The TT Max is big, but it's not too big by any means. It serves as a reminder that the Switch 2 is a legitimate current-gen console, easily on par with something like the Xbox Series S, but with additional mobile functionality. The Switch 2 is a little hybrid device that's capable of handling any AAA game you throw at it, including third-party monsters like Elden Ring, Cyberpunk 2077, Resident Evil Requiem, Street Fighter 6, Diablo IV and so on. And if you do come across a game that you'd rather play on PC, the TT Max can follow you there, too.

title_en: Microsoft says it made Windows 11 zippier, especially on PCs with less RAM
title_fa: Microsoft says it made Windows 11 zippier, especially on PCs with less RAM
excerpt_en: The whole RAM price thing is partly Microsoft's fault so it's the least it can do.
excerpt_fa: The whole RAM price thing is partly Microsoft's fault so it's the least it can do.
content_en:
Microsoft says it made Windows 11 zippier, especially on PCs with less RAM
The company also unveiled a revamped Photos app that testers can try now.
Microsoft has been working on some Windows 11 updates that it's starting to bring to all users after testing them with Windows Insiders. Among other things, the company said it made the operating system up to 20 percent more responsive, in part by improving memory efficiency and management. For instance, Windows 11 "can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, helping your PC stay responsive as you open more apps or browser tabs," Navjot Virk, Microsoft's corporate vice president of Windows Experiences, wrote in a blog post.
Virk noted that PCs with 8GB of memory may see "an especially meaningful difference." That's welcome, given that it's increasingly expensive to upgrade RAM in a PC. You can largely blame AI data centers for gobbling up as much memory as possible and jacking up prices for normal people. Microsoft, of course, is heavily involved in that, so improved memory management and efficiency feels like the least the company can do to mitigate the RAM crisis.
One thing Windows 11 will do on PCs with 8GB or less of RAM is to only load widgets when users actually open them. Microsoft says that'll free up over 200MB of memory for other tasks.
Microsoft says it should also be faster to pair AirPods with PCs as part of improvements to Bluetooth headphone reliability. Windows Hello logins are said to be easier, faster and more reliable too.
Windows Insider testers can now try out the revamped, AI-powered Search that the company unveiled last week. They can carry out thousands of actions directly through Search, which Microsoft is effectively turning into a chatbot.
Other updates for Insiders include a new Photos app with a revamped gallery that can pull together snaps from local storage, OneDrive and iCloud. The built-in editor is said to load 25 percent faster. The native viewer loads 30 percent quicker too, Microsoft claims.

title_en: AI agents are coming to Rivian’s cars
title_fa: AI agents are coming to Rivian’s cars
excerpt_en: We'll likely learn more about how this will work at the company's upcoming "AI & Autonomy Day" event in December.
excerpt_fa: We'll likely learn more about how this will work at the company's upcoming "AI & Autonomy Day" event in December.
content_en:
Rivian recently rolled out an AI assistant that lets drivers and passengers interact with the company’s electric vehicles just by talking to them. But the carmaker’s founder and CEO, RJ Scaringe, said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that, in the future, Rivian’s cars will be able to run AI agents made by other companies like Anthropic.
“That’s where it becomes magical,” Scaringe said onstage.
Scaringe didn’t say when Rivian would implement this, and the company declined to offer more details, pointing instead to the “AI & Autonomy Day” event it’s hosting in December.
But it’s not hard to imagine how Rivian might integrate something like Claude, OpenAI’s Dots, or Meta’s Muse assistant into its software. The company has developed its in-car software from the ground up, instead of leaning on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and built a lot of its own applications, like navigation (though it has worked to integrate popular in-car apps like Apple Music).
Rivian says it has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. Most of the time, that involves what you’d expect: asking the car to turn down the temperature, activate the seat warmers, or summarize the news.
“Think of it as like a traffic light. So if you ask the vehicle something, it decides what model it’s going to use. It can use a local model that’s running on the edge and the vehicle. If it’s a more complex question, it can go up to the cloud. And then even for that, we have different models that we use,” Scaringe said.
As of May of this year, the agent could access external apps like Google Calendar. And Scaringe said at Disrupt the next step would be to add products from the frontier AI companies, though making them work in the car won’t be easy.
“There’s a lot of plumbing behind the scenes we have to do to make sure that that works, and it’s not just within Rivian. That’s also a lot of coordination with the labs to make sure they enable that plumbing,” he said, adding that putting this kind of software near safety-critical systems means Rivian has to be extremely careful.
“You wouldn’t want an agent to determine, ‘hey, it’s time to apply the brakes, or time to steer the vehicle.’ So anything that’s vehicle-level controls are not being handed to an agent,” he said.
Instead, he thinks the implementation will look more like an extension of how people currently use these agentic apps. That would mean Rivian would have to find a way to connect the vehicle to all of the context that apps like Muse collect on their users.
For example, Scaringe said, a driver could ask the Rivian assistant to turn on the ventilated seats before going deeper. “And then simultaneously say, ‘We were talking yesterday about this meal. I’m planning to have guests over on Friday. Can you help me think through what we’re going to make?’,” he said. The car could then pull the driver’s context from a conversation they had with the assistant on another device.
Of course, Rivian wouldn’t be the first American car company to add AI agents to a car’s software. Earlier this year, Tesla added a feature that let users talk to both SpaceX’s Grok chatbot and also its Grok Bot assistant.

title_en: Ramp reaches $60B valuation as it pushes deeper into AI
title_fa: Ramp reaches $60B valuation as it pushes deeper into AI
excerpt_en: The funding comes as Ramp's annualized revenue crosses $2B, and its customer count reaches 85,000.
excerpt_fa: The funding comes as Ramp's annualized revenue crosses $2B, and its customer count reaches 85,000.
content_en:
Expense management company Ramp said on Thursday that it had raised $1.85 billion in a new funding round that values it at $60 billion, just four months after raising $750 million at a $44 billion valuation.
The financing was co-led by Dragoneer Investment Group, Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Sands Capital, and Avenir Growth.
Ramp said its annualized revenue has crossed $2 billion, up from a reported $1.5 billion in June, and that its revenue growth is 25% faster than it was around this time last year. The company claims it now facilitates annualized purchase volume of over $275 billion, up 175% from a year earlier. It also says it has 85,000 customers, up from 70,000 in June, including Visa, Uber, Shopify, Robinhood, Anduril, Notion, Cursor, and Figma.
The funding comes as Ramp has been expanding beyond expense management into payments, fraud detection, procurement, vendor management, and, of late, even accounting.
The startup has also built an AI story around itself, embedding AI agents into its procurement, expense management, accounting, budgeting, and other products. It also launched a corporate credit card specifically designed for AI agents to use, and in August entered the model routing business to tap the booming AI inference market and give existing clients a model routing service that fits neatly with its current products, including AI token usage monitoring and token spend management.
Earlier this month, Ramp launched Glass, a workspace that collects and remembers the AI automations, prompts, and skills that an organization’s employees build so others can take advantage of the company’s collective knowledge and skills.
“In just a few years, Ramp has become a much broader financial operations platform, with AI deeply embedded in how the company builds and operates. We believe Ramp is well on its way to becoming one of the defining companies of this era,” Christian Jensen, partner at Dragoneer, said in a statement.
Other investors in the round include Capital International, Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, D1 Capital Partners, Greenoaks, ICONIQ, GIC, 8VC, 1789 Capital, Alpha Wave Global, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Coatue, D.E. Shaw, Definition Capital, FirstMark, General Catalyst, Generation Investment Management, Glade Brook Capital Partners, Khosla Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Pinegrove Opportunity Partners, Soma Capital, and Stripes.
The company has now raised about $5 billion in funding.
As Ramp has widened its product lineup, it has increasingly run into Rippling, the HR and payroll software company that has pushed into corporate cards, expense management, and bill payments. The overlap puts the two companies in direct competition for the same finance-team budgets.
Early investor Keith Rabois, who has backed Ramp through two firms, Founders Fund and Khosla Ventures, both of which participated in this round, spoke to TechCrunch last month about Ramp’s strategy and his own big ambitions for the company.
“Ramp is not worried about Rippling,” Rabois said. “We’re going to compete with Anthropic,” he continued. “That’s the goal. I want to be larger and more successful and more important than Anthropic. Ramp is going to be the primary way people manage their token spend, how they optimize it, how they measure ROI, and that will lead us to collide probably with Anthropic in many ways.”
— With additional reporting from Connie Loizos

title_en: Google’s Universal Cart shopping tool launches in the US
title_fa: Google’s Universal Cart shopping tool launches in the US
excerpt_en: The new shopping tool is available in the U.S. across Google Search and the Gemini app.
excerpt_fa: The new shopping tool is available in the U.S. across Google Search and the Gemini app.
content_en:
Google on Thursday said “Universal Cart,” a tool that lets users collect and monitor products they find across search and in the Gemini app, is now available to U.S. users. The company first previewed the tool at Google I/O in May.
The idea is to make online shopping easier to manage. Find something you like, save it to your cart, and move on. When you return later, your items and shopping progress are still there, so you don’t have to hunt down the same products or start over. Universal Cart can collect items from multiple retailers, turning it into a central hub for browsing and keeping track of potential purchases.
Google says the cart can also help shoppers stay on top of deals and availability. The tool can send notifications when a saved product’s price drops or when an out-of-stock item becomes available again.
The tool is also designed to offer more tailored help during the shopping process. Google says it can take credit card perks into account when helping users choose how to pay, and also surface relevant promo codes.
Checkout is tied to Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP, an open standard the company introduced earlier this year. UCP is designed to help AI agents and retailers work together across different parts of the shopping journey, including checkout.
Google is already deeply invested in AI-powered shopping, and Universal Cart is its latest effort to make the experience more convenient. It joins features such as conversational product discovery in Search’s AI Mode and Google’s “Let Google Call” tool, which uses an AI agent to contact nearby stores and check whether an item is in stock.
Google isn’t the only company bringing AI into e-commerce. Amazon, OpenAI, and other rivals have added agentic commerce features as companies look for ways to make chatbots useful beyond answering questions.

title_en: Opera's lightweight Air browser is back, unbothered, moisturized, in its lane
title_fa: Opera's lightweight Air browser is back, unbothered, moisturized, in its lane
excerpt_en: Namaste.
excerpt_fa: Namaste.
content_en:
Opera's lightweight Air browser is back, unbothered, moisturized, in its lane
New soundtracks and breathing exercises are designed to encourage mindful browsing.
Opera has relaunched its very mindful Air browser with a host of new anti-distraction features. The audiovisual makeover is designed to help you focus better on what you're actually supposed to be doing, rather than encouraging you to wander into yet another free time-draining Reddit rabbit hole.
The first new addition is music. Opera seemingly knows that people turn to ambient playlists when they're trying to concentrate, so it's built its own. Air Soundscapes give the browser a soundtrack split into four moods: Focus, Relax, Work and Ambience. Pick the latter and you'll be treated to the tranquil sounds of forests and the sea.
Opera Air also now has built-in breathing exercises, which you can schedule to pop up at your chosen intervals, as well as neck stretches you can follow along to.
The Air browser is purposefully streamlined, so you have to manually add any apps you want to the sidebar. Opera has added new wallpapers that it says incorporate "open spaces, perspective and natural textures" to make your browsing experience as serene as possible. It also now has an automatic dark mode.
Given its resistance to the many distractions of the web, Air naturally has a built-in ad blocker, and you even get a free VPN. It does interface with ChatGPT but that sidebar option is unchecked by default. The resigned user experience builds on the first version of Air that Opera introduced in early 2025 as a mindful antidote to the chaos of the internet.
Opera Air remains free to download on Windows and macOS.

Opera's lightweight Air browser is back, unbothered, moisturized, in its lane
New soundtracks and breathing exercises are designed to encourage mindful browsing.
Opera has relaunched its very mindful Air browser with a host of new anti-distraction features. The audiovisual makeover is designed to help you focus better on what you're actually supposed to be doing, rather than encouraging you to wander into yet another free time-draining Reddit rabbit hole.
The first new addition is music. Opera seemingly knows that people turn to ambient playlists when they're trying to concentrate, so it's built its own. Air Soundscapes give the browser a soundtrack split into four moods: Focus, Relax, Work and Ambience. Pick the latter and you'll be treated to the tranquil sounds of forests and the sea.
Opera Air also now has built-in breathing exercises, which you can schedule to pop up at your chosen intervals, as well as neck stretches you can follow along to.
The Air browser is purposefully streamlined, so you have to manually add any apps you want to the sidebar. Opera has added new wallpapers that it says incorporate "open spaces, perspective and natural textures" to make your browsing experience as serene as possible. It also now has an automatic dark mode.
Given its resistance to the many distractions of the web, Air naturally has a built-in ad blocker, and you even get a free VPN. It does interface with ChatGPT but that sidebar option is unchecked by default. The resigned user experience builds on the first version of Air that Opera introduced in early 2025 as a mindful antidote to the chaos of the internet.
Opera Air remains free to download on Windows and macOS.

Tesla Roadster reveal live: Updates from the launch of the next-gen sportscar
Elon Musk has been saying the demo might be a literal "banger."
It's been about nine years since Tesla introduced an updated version of its Roadster electric sports car in 2017, saying it would be ready in 2020. After repeated delays over the years, the company is finally ready to unveil its second-gen hypercar. That's supposed to happen tonight (October 15) at 8:55PM ET — that is, if the company doesn't delay things again.
CEO Elon Musk has already been posting about the vehicle on X, claiming, among other things, that "The new Tesla Roadster is a candidate for greatest product demo of all time." The company has certainly promised some intriguing features at the 2017 reveal, including a 620-mile range and the ability to go from zero to 60 in 1.9 seconds.
More recently, images on Tesla's website teasing the new Roadster seem to imply the possibility of cold-gas thrusters. Reports also indicated that it might have the ability to fly. Musk has also posted on X that "Let's just say that this demo will be a BANGER, probably metaphorically, though some chance literally."
There will clearly be a lot of spectacle to witness later today, and we can't wait to watch it all with you. We will be kicking off this liveblog at about 4PM ET, and are looking forward to reading your comments while we all wait to see if Tesla actually delivers today.
107 Updates

Hello everyone and welcome to our liveblog of today's Tesla Roadster reveal event. Despite all the stops and starts over the years, it seems like the company actually might go ahead and unveil its second-gen sportscar today. That is, if Elon Musk's frenzied posting on X is anything to go by.
-
I see there are already a lot of you in our comments section, and 40 of you have left messages. One of you only said "test" — is that a sign of things to come tonight? I will say that one of my favorite comments so far is by "songbirdsnake," who said "We're getting a flying car before GTA 6!" followed closely by "chase" with a GIF of a skeleton.
-
Karissa just discovered and confirmed that the Roadster easter egg described in this tweet actually works:
Tesla just updated the Roadster Easter Egg on the website.
When you flip the Roadster upside down, and adjust the photo settings, it now says:
" ⬆️ THIS SIDE UP ⬆️ " pic.twitter.com/Jx289YdZ6y
— Nic Cruz Patane (@niccruzpatane) October 15, 2026
-
It looks like we have a mix of Tesla (or Musk) fans as well as cynics and skeptics (or realists?) in our comments section, which feels like a solid representation of the internet at large. I was expecting plenty of EV enthusiasts here, but I appreciate when people share their real, lived experiences of buying cars in this economy.
As a Singaporean, my understanding of car prices is completely skewed, but even I find it wild that there are people who paid $50,000 as deposits for this vehicle back in 2017. If any of you here did that, please let us know below whether you canceled your order or held on!
-
Commenter by the name "Gizmo-No!" (very funny name lol) said "Vaporware until I see one on the street." along with some other great observations that I'm not sure I can repeat verbatim? Anyway, I just wanted to say I appreciate the username.
-
Oh I saw this comment earlier today and honestly it's probably my favorite comment of the day. "I hope they used stronger glue on this car than they did on the Cyberdumpster." by "8647" I hope that's your PIN code for something!
-
In case you all haven't been on X (I wouldn't blame you), here's something Musk posted this morning:
New Roadster is
beyond movies,
beyond imagination,
beyond human,
yet still made
by humans
on Earth— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 15, 2026
-
Ooh I'm intrigued by the very intelligent guesses made by commenter "Frank Durocher," who says
"My predictions in order of craziest to most mundane...
Sensationalized prediction: they drop this out of a plane and it lands on stage like Starship.
More fun, but reasonable prediction: The rumors about downforce creation (and their teaser images being upside down) play into the car having so much downforce that they drive it to the stage upside-down, stuck to the ceiling.
Boring prediction: The thrusters help it accelerate faster and cost so much money that they're not available to the general public.
And why 7:55pm CST? Maybe it has 755hp."
-
There's about 3 hours and 40 minutes to go before the livestream is scheduled to begin. That's plenty of time to get dinner (or whatever meal makes sense for you), a nap and maybe even a walk. If you would prefer to watch the livestream for yourself, you can do so on X. If you don't want to for any reason, we'll be here for you!
-
Here's a picture the Tesla account posted to X today.
-
I see we have a live one! Commenter "Sagey" says Tesla has had their deposit for four years! You have an abundance of faith, tenacity and, I'm assuming, money? I would be curious how you feel by the end of the night! Elated, disappointed or relieved?
-
While we're on a liveblog about Tesla, there's been speculation that the company might merge with SpaceX. Analysts at Barclays wrote a note that indicated they believed an announcement about the deal could be made as soon as later this month.
-
Hello! I do think it's likely a matter of "when" not "if" we will see the ultimate consolidation with SpaceXAI (or is it SpaceXSI?) and Tesla. It would certainly cement Musk's control over all his companies. I appreciate this line from that Barclays memo: "The true value would be in vertical integration." Isn't it always? (I am going to show my age here, but there is a very funny 30 Rock bit about vertical integration I always think of when I see the phrase.)
-
Really enjoying some of these reader predictions. I'm personally wondering if that teaser isn't pointing at a recreation of the classic Mercedes-Benz SLS AMG ad where it briefly drives upside-down through a tunnel:
-
How's...

The final day of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 has arrived, and the week is ending on a high note. As 10,000+ founders, investors, and technology leaders gather at San Francisco’s Moscone West, Day 3 features some of the conference’s most practical and future-focused discussions.
Explore sessions covering the next wave of AI innovation, startup growth strategies, fundraising, emerging technologies, and lessons from the entrepreneurs and investors defining the future of tech. Add in Startup Battlefield excitement, peer networking, and countless opportunities for serendipitous connections, and it’s one final opportunity to maximize your Disrupt experience.
Don’t miss your chance to be part of the conversations everyone will be talking about after Disrupt. Grab your pass now at 75% off the original ticket price and join us for Day 3.
Day 3 highlights
Registration hours: 8:00 a.m. – 3:30 p.m.
Stop by the registration desk in the Level 1 lobby of Moscone West to register in person or pick up your scannable event badge. The badge features Klik technology, which makes it easy to exchange contact information with people you scan your badge with. Using the event app, you can access and keep those contacts even after the event ends.
Expo Hall: 8:00 a.m. – 3:30 p.m.
Explore 320+ exhibiting startups showcasing cutting-edge technologies across industries. This is the center of Disrupt, where 10,000+ attendees converge to discover new breakthroughs and spark new connections.
Haven’t registered yet? You still can — but don’t wait, or you will miss out. title_en: LinkedIn is adding new tools to help people with their side hustles
title_fa: LinkedIn is adding new tools to help people with their side hustles
excerpt_en: The company says more of its users are holding down multiple roles.
excerpt_fa: The company says more of its users are holding down multiple roles.
content_en:
LinkedIn is adding new tools to help people with their side hustles
The company says more of its users are holding down multiple roles.
LinkedIn is adding a bunch of new features meant to help people keep up with their side hustles, vibe-coding projects and other pursuits that might not align with their day job. The company is tweaking profiles so people can highlight multiple jobs and introducing new creator-focused tools for founders.
Some of the changes are meant to make it easier for people to keep up with people they actually know on the platform. The service is testing a "network" feed that will only show posts and updates from existing connections and accounts you follow, rather than algorithmic recommendations. And it's adding a "business card" feature that can be added to your phone's wallet app to make it easier to connect on LinkedIn with people you meet IRL.
Founders and business owners will also have a new way to monetize their LinkedIn presence with something called "Advice Sessions." The feature will allow people to offer paid one-on-one meetings and consultations through the platform. The company says the feature will initially be available to those with a business premium subscription in the US, and that it won't take a cut of users' earnings from these sessions.
LinkedIn is introducing other creator-centric tools too, including a new analytics dashboard so people can better understand how their posts are performing. For creators making video content, the platform plans to expand its revenue-sharing program that passes on a cut of revenue generated by pre-roll ads.
All of the changes, according to LinkedIn, are meant to reflect the fact that work looks different now for a lot of people, thanks to the rise of AI. The company says it's seen a 70-percent increase in people who have added "founder" to their profiles over the last year, and that more people are listing multiple ongoing roles in their profiles.
I asked the company's Chief Product Officer, Hari Srinivasan, if that's because AI is making it easier and faster to start a new venture or if disruptions in the labor market from AI are forcing people to get more creative. He said the company's data shows "there are definitely more people starting businesses now," though it's "hard to tell" what the underlying reasons for that may be.
He also noted that there's more to starting a new venture than simply vibe coding a piece of software. "You can build all this incredible stuff with AI, but I don't know if it's necessarily made it easier to build a business."

title_en: NVIDIA's RTX Spark is good for Windows, even if you don't need local AI
title_fa: NVIDIA's RTX Spark is good for Windows, even if you don't need local AI
excerpt_en: NVIDIA's RTX Spark is meant for AI fiends, but it could end up helping Windows PCs in general
excerpt_fa: NVIDIA's RTX Spark is meant for AI fiends, but it could end up helping Windows PCs in general
content_en:
NVIDIA's RTX Spark is good for Windows, even if you don't need local AI
Windows PCs may finally catch up to Apple Silicon.
Last week, I spent two days hearing how Microsoft and NVIDIA are "reinventing the PC" with RTX Spark, the new system-on-a-chip powering the Surface Laptop Ultra and several other Windows PCs this fall. It's the first time we've seen powerful Arm CPUs joined together with NVIDIA's Blackwell GPU technology and up to 128GB of ultra-fast unified memory on a single chip. Theoretically, RTX Spark should allow for thin-yet-powerful laptops (and a few small desktops) that can handle AI tasks locally, as well as tackling content creation and gaming. So sure, I suppose NVIDIA and Microsoft have a reason to gloat a bit.
But, just like the launch of Snapdragon-powered Copilot+ systems two years ago, it was hard to ignore the elephant in the room: RTX Spark is clearly a response to Apple Silicon and the transformational changes it brought to Macs six years ago. Apple's chips are also made up of a powerful Arm CPU, capable GPU and fast unified memory, and they span the company's lineup from the tiny Mac mini to the super-powerful Mac Studio and 16-inch MacBook Pro. With RTX Spark, Windows users finally have a way to see the benefits of an efficient Arm-based SoC on high-end PCs, while the recent batch of Qualcomm chips covers the low-end and mid-range.
There weren't many surprises at Microsoft's AI launch event (featuring the Surface Laptop Ultra), or at NVIDIA's RTX Spark Editor's Day, which I attended alongside other media and analysts. Both companies want to sell us a future where we can run AI models and agents right from an RTX Spark-powered Windows laptop, something that seemed clear since the chip was announced at Computex. But even if that future doesn't come to pass, RTX Spark could still lead to some intriguing changes in the PC world.
Under the hood with RTX Spark
The RTX Spark SoC is powered by up to 20 NVIDIA Grace Arm CPU cores (10 performance cores and 10 efficiency cores), a Blackwell GPU with up to 6,144 CUDA cores, and up to 128GB of unified LPDDR5x memory running at 9,400 Mbps. There's also a slightly less powerful configuration with 18 CPU cores and 5,120 GPU cores. RTX Spark also includes much of what you'd find on NVIDIA's latest GPUs, including fifth-gen tensor cores, fourth-gen ray tracing cores, and a Blackwell video engine (with support of AV1 UHQ and 4:2:2 encoding and decoding).
By shoving all of this hardware onto a single chip, NVIDIA claims the RTX Spark is twice as efficient as a laptop powered by an Intel Core Ultra 9 285H and RTX 5070 dedicated GPU, while gaming at 60 watts. NVIDIA has previously said RTX Spark systems should be similarly powerful to RTX 5070 laptops, though as you can tell from the chart below, those dedicated GPU systems can also draw a lot more energy for better performance.
If you plan to be connected to power most of the time and don't need to travel with your laptop, you may see little benefit from choosing an RTX Spark system. But if you need to do serious creative work on the go, RTX Spark's improved efficiency allows PCs to work as fast on battery as they are while plugged in, according to NVIDIA. From my brief time with the Surface Laptop Ultra, I didn't notice any performance drops while playing Gears of War: E-Day on battery power. The game still looked silky smooth in 1440p with high graphics settings.
RTX Spark is built for AI, but also helps content creation and gaming
With its support for tons of unified RAM, RTX Spark systems should appeal to AI developers and researchers who need as much memory as they can to run large AI models locally, like the 125B parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. An RTX Spark system could significantly reduce the amount of money spent on cloud AI tokens, or replace that demand entirely. One researcher I spoke with was jealous that his colleagues were able to easily run AI models on modern Mac laptops, and he was excited about the possibility of doing the same on a Windows notebook. RTX Spark is also coming along as Microsoft is adding more support in Windows 11 for on-device AI tools like Perplexity, as well as simplified ways to set up AI agents like OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot.
Not surprisingly, NVIDIA is also touting RTX Spark's gaming capabilities. Since it features a Blackwell GPU front and center, it'll deliver all of the features you'd expect from RTX 50-series cards, including support for DLSS 5. As I mentioned before, you can expect performance similar to an RTX 5070 — NVIDIA is specifically touting 1440p as the intended resolution for RTX Spark systems, though I'd be interested to see how they perform in 4K with DLSS. A new performance mode for DLSS Frame Generation can push Cyberpunk 2077 up to 280fps with 6x frame gen, compared 213fps without performance mode. (It's unclear what you lose to achieve that frame bump, though.)
Since RTX Spark is Arm-based, it won't natively run every game on Windows, but NVIDIA claims recent titles like Control Resonant and the aforementioned Gears of War: E-Day will be supported at launch thanks to Microsoft's Prism emulator for x86 software. NBA 2K27, the main DLSS 5 launch game, will also be supported, alongside World of Warcraft: Forever. NVIDIA says it's also working with major anti-cheat providers to support their products, something that's prevented multiplayer games from working on Arm Windows systems in the past.
I'll have to spend more time with RTX Spark systems to see how well they actually handle gaming, beyond my minutes with Gears of War: E-Day. But if playing games is a priority, you'd still be better off with an Intel or AMD system with a dedicated GPU. At least then you wouldn't have to worry about potential emulation issues.
RTX Spark systems will also be useful content creation — again, as you'd expect from PCs with RTX Blackwell GPUs. You can lean on hardware acceleration in tools like Blender, and notably, Adobe is re-architecting...

title_en: Xreal's new flagship One Pro+ AR glasses offer better brightness and increased comfort
title_fa: Xreal's new flagship One Pro+ AR glasses offer better brightness and increased comfort
excerpt_en: There's still no camera here, so they won't be confused for pervert specs.
excerpt_fa: There's still no camera here, so they won't be confused for pervert specs.
content_en:
Xreal's new flagship One Pro+ AR glasses offer better brightness and increased comfort
There's still no camera here, so they won't be confused for pervert specs.
Xreal just released an upgrade of its popular One Pro AR glasses. The One Pro+ is a minor refresh, but offers some welcome quality of life improvements.
First of all, it's brighter than ever before. The One Pro+ reaches 1,200 nits of peak brightness, compared to 700 nits for the standard One Pro. It also includes AI HDR upscaling tech to improve the visuals.The company has upgraded its 2D-to-3D conversion algorithm from 30Hz to 60Hz. This is for adding depth to 2D content, which is similar to the spatial imaging system available with the Apple Vision Pro.
Finally, there's a newly designed nose pad to maximize long-term comfort. The company promises this pad will improve overall stability, but not at the expense of field of view. This is actually the feature I'm most excited about because there's a huge difference between wearing AR glasses for 20 minutes and hunkering down for two or three hours of work. They tend to get uncomfortable pretty fast.
Other than that, these are still Xreal One Pro glasses. They offer the same X1 spatial computing chip and a 57-degree field of view. This is not a bad thing, as we enjoyed the original One Pro. They are great for productivity, via screen mirroring, and watching stuff. We actually said they intrigued us in ways that Meta's glasses never did.
To that end, there's one missing feature here that's a mainstay with Meta. The Xreal One Pro+ AR glasses do not have a camera, so people are unlikely to suspect you are wearing pervert glasses. Xreal's new specs are available right now and cost $600, which is the same price as last year's One Pro.

title_en: CitizenLab details new spyware triggered by online advertising
title_fa: CitizenLab details new spyware triggered by online advertising
excerpt_en: A new type of spyware dubbed "AdFection" is infecting phones and computers via global online advertising networks.
excerpt_fa: A new type of spyware dubbed "AdFection" is infecting phones and computers via global online advertising networks.
content_en:
CitizenLab details new spyware triggered by online advertising
It requires 'no interaction' from victims to infect devices.
A new type of spyware dubbed "AdFection" is infecting phones and computers via global online advertising networks, according to a new report from Citizen Lab. The attack is unique in that it can infect devices just by showing an ad, with no need for the victim to click on a link or file. The researchers said that AdFection is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads.
The ad-infiltrating technology was reportedly developed by Israeli company called Discover-Tech. Researchers said it has been used to target journalists and staff at the Al Jazeera news network, along with officials and employees at organizations including NATO, the European Commission, NVIDIA and Arm.
"Discover-Tech has leveraged the advertising ecosystem for years to turn trusted websites and popular apps into a zero-click spyware delivery platform," Citizen Lab senior researcher Bill Marczak told The Financial Times. Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm but instead serves as a "bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem," Citizen Lab's report states
Google was among the major ad platforms targeted by the spyware, but it has now suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list. "Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies," the company said in a statement.
Targeted online advertising is a highly desirable medium to spread malware because it's prevalent on the web globally. It works though an automated real-time bidding auction system that lets advertisers compete to show ads to specific internet users. Discover-Tech's software used the system instead to profile and de-anonymize such users before targeting them with spyware, the report states. Victims were then sent malicious malware code buried in innocent-looking ads.
Discover-Tech reportedly displayed 442 million ads on more than 120,000 websites, including the BBC and New York Times, along with mobile apps like Duolingo, Badoo and Grindr. The ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure and national cyber agencies. Citizen Lab researchers found login records on Discover-Tech's site, including details belonging to employees of the spyware maker Candiru.
The discovery is "surely just the tip of the iceberg," Marczak said in the blog post. "If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it's time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether." Discover-Tech and other players in the scheme have yet to comment.
